benefits: Builds the obliques and abdominals through the rotation pattern.; Develops core endurance and rotational strength.; Trains the core anywhere with no equipment needed.
useCases: Core finisher slots in ab-focused fitness apps; Rotational athlete training blocks for sport platforms; Beginner ab onboarding flows in coaching apps; Reels and short-form core content for fitness creators
instructions: 1. Sit on the floor with your knees bent and your feet flat on the ground in front of you. ; 2. Lean back until your torso is at about a 45-degree angle and brace your core hard. ; 3. Lift your feet a few inches off the floor and balance on your sit bones with shins parallel to the ground. ; 4. Clasp your hands together in front of your chest and rotate your torso to one side under control. ; 5. Tap your hands lightly to the floor beside your hip, feeling the oblique on that side contract. ; 6. Rotate smoothly to the other side and tap, alternating for the prescribed reps without dropping the feet.
commonMistakes: Just swinging the arms side to side without rotating the torso — loads the shoulders, not the core.; Rounding the back instead of staying tall through the spine, which strains the lower back.; Letting the feet drop to the floor every rep, which breaks the constant core tension.; Rushing the tempo instead of pausing on each side — turns a controlled twist into momentum-only work.
shortDescription: A seated rotational core exercise that twists side to side — the most recognizable oblique builder in any ab program.
longDescription:
The bodyweight Russian twist is the most recognized rotational core exercise in any ab program. Sitting balanced on the glutes with the feet lifted, the torso rotates side to side under tension. It trains the obliques and abdominals through the rotation pattern that the rest of the core program usually misses.

For fitness apps, Russian twists are a staple inclusion in any ab circuit, core finisher, or rotational athlete training block. They scale endlessly with tempo, foot position, or added load (medicine ball or plate). Use this clip in beginner ab onboarding, sport-specific rotation programs, and core finisher modules across your library.

name: Bodyweight Spinal Jefferson Curl
tags: jefferson curl; spinal mobility; flexibility; bodyweight; back stretch; mobility
benefits: Improves spinal mobility through a full forward-fold range.; Stretches the hamstrings, glutes, and entire back of the body.; Builds resilience and control in a flexed spine position.
useCases: Mobility-focused flexibility programs in fitness apps; Recovery and cooldown flows for strength training apps; Yoga-adjacent content in wellness platforms; Lifter mobility modules in coaching apps
instructions: 1. Stand tall on a flat surface with feet hip-width apart and arms hanging in front of your thighs. ; 2. Tuck your chin to your chest and start rolling down slowly, one vertebra at a time. ; 3. Continue folding forward through the upper back, then mid-back, then lower back as you descend. ; 4. Let your arms hang relaxed in front of your shins and reach for the floor without straining. ; 5. Pause briefly at the bottom, feeling the stretch through the entire back of the body. ; 6. Reverse the motion by rolling back up segment by segment until you stand fully tall again.
commonMistakes: Folding from the hips only instead of rounding the spine — defeats the entire point of the drill.; Bending the knees too much, which removes the hamstring stretch and shortens the load on the back.; Going too heavy too soon — this is a mobility tool, not a strength lift.; Snapping back up to standing instead of rolling up segment by segment under control.
shortDescription: A slow, segmented forward fold that mobilizes the entire spine — the gymnastics-staple flexibility drill for stiff backs.
longDescription:
The Jefferson curl is a spinal-mobility exercise borrowed from gymnastics and dance training. By rolling slowly down through each vertebra in a deep forward fold, it loads the spine in flexion through a full range and stretches the entire back of the body. Done with light load and high control, it builds back resilience and spinal mobility most users never train.

For app builders, this is a standout addition to mobility libraries, yoga-adjacent flexibility programs, and lifter-recovery tracks. It is also useful as a bridge piece between strength and mobility content. Ship it in flexibility blocks and recovery flows where users want to feel a real opening through the back rather than another generic stretch.

name: Bodyweight Squat
tags: bodyweight squat; squat pattern; leg exercise; bodyweight; beginner; lower body
benefits: Builds the quads, glutes, and inner thighs with no equipment.; Teaches the foundational squat pattern for every loaded variation.; Improves lower-body mobility and balance in any setting.
useCases: Onboarding squat education in fitness apps; Warm-up flows for leg-day strength programs; Beginner home workouts in coaching platforms; Movement-screen modules in personal training tools
instructions: 1. Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart and your toes pointed slightly outward. ; 2. Brace your core, lift your chest, and extend your arms straight out for balance. ; 3. Sit your hips back and down as if lowering into a chair, keeping your weight in your heels. ; 4. Lower until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor, with knees tracking over your toes. ; 5. Keep your chest tall and your spine neutral throughout the descent — no rounding at the bottom. ; 6. Drive through your heels to stand back up, squeezing your glutes hard at the top of the rep.
commonMistakes: Letting the knees cave inward, which weakens the squat and loads the knee joint badly.; Squatting straight down instead of sitting the hips back, which puts all the work on the knees.; Lifting the heels off the floor at the bottom, which kills balance and reduces glute drive.; Cutting the depth short and squatting only halfway — robs the lift of glute and quad work.
shortDescription: The foundational squat pattern done with just bodyweight — the first leg exercise in any program and the test of clean mechanics.
longDescription:
The bodyweight squat is the foundational leg pattern in human movement. By sitting the hips back and down with the chest tall, it trains the quads, glutes, and inner thighs through a full hip-and-knee bend. It is the clearest test of squat mechanics any program can use, and the prerequisite for every loaded squat variation that comes later.

For any fitness app, this clip is non-negotiable inventory. It belongs in every onboarding flow, every beginner program, every warm-up sequence, and every movement-screen module. Ship it in your core library and use it as a teaching anchor for the entire squat family — from goblet squats to barbell back squats.

name: Box Jump
tags: box jump; plyometric; explosive power; bodyweight; athletic training; lower body
benefits: Builds explosive lower-body power for sport and athletic performance.; Trains reactive strength with reduced landing impact.; Develops glute, quad, and calf power through triple extension.
useCases: Athletic prep blocks in sport performance apps; Plyometric training modules for hybrid fitness platforms; HIIT and conditioning workout flows in fitness apps; Vertical jump training content for basketball and volleyball creators
instructions: 1. Stand a comfortable distance in front of a sturdy box with feet shoulder-width apart. ; 2. Drop into a quarter squat by sitting your hips back and swinging your arms behind you. ; 3. Explode upward by driving through the floor and swinging your arms forward and up. ; 4. Pull your knees up underneath you in mid-air and aim to land softly on top of the box. ; 5. Land in a soft quarter squat with both feet flat on the box and your chest tall. ; 6. Stand fully tall on top of the box, then step down one leg at a time and reset for the next rep.
commonMistakes: Jumping down from the box instead of stepping down — adds unnecessary impact to the knees over volume.; Landing with stiff legs and a flat impact instead of absorbing softly into a quarter squat.; Choosing a box too tall and barely clearing it, which leads to scraped shins and missed reps.; Using too much arm swing without leg drive — turns a power lift into an arm-thrown jump.
shortDescription: An explosive jump from the floor onto a box — the clean way to train lower-body power without high-impact landings.
longDescription:
The box jump is one of the most efficient plyometric exercises in any athletic program. By exploding off the floor and landing on a sturdy box, it trains lower-body power and reactive strength while keeping landing impact low — the box absorbs what would otherwise be a hard floor landing. It builds the glutes, quads, and calves through fast, powerful triple extension.

For app builders, this clip belongs in any conditioning, athletic prep, or hybrid training program. It is a clean fit for sport-performance modules — basketball, volleyball, sprinting — where vertical power transfers directly. Use it in HIIT workout flows and explosive-strength accessory blocks where coaches want a power lift that does not require a barbell.

name: Breaststroke Swim
tags: breaststroke; swimming; cardio; whip kick; low impact; pool
benefits: Builds a low-impact aerobic pattern with a clear, teachable rhythm.; Loads the inner thigh and hip musculature harder than the other strokes.; Allows a breath every cycle, which makes pacing straightforward for beginners.
useCases: Stroke selection screens in a swim app.; Learn-to-swim technique modules that teach stroke timing.; Low-impact cardio programming for joint-sensitive users.; Muscle-highlight content contrasting the four competitive strokes.
instructions: 1. Float face down with your body straight and arms extended in front of you. ; 2. Sweep both hands outward then back toward the midline in a circle, keeping the elbows high. ; 3. Lift your head and shoulders to inhale as the arms complete the pull. ; 4. Recover the hands together ahead of your shoulders, then shoot them forward. ; 5. Draw your heels toward your seat, turn your feet out and whip them back together. ; 6. Hold the streamlined glide until speed drops, then start the next cycle.
commonMistakes: Pulling too wide and too far back, which stalls the stroke and overloads the shoulders.; Kicking with the feet pointed instead of turned out, which removes most of the propulsion.; Cutting the glide short, so stroke rate rises and efficiency falls.; Lifting the head too early, which drops the hips and drags the body line.
shortDescription: Prone simultaneous-stroke swimming that pairs a wide sweeping arm pull with a whip kick driven by the inner thighs.
longDescription:
Breaststroke runs on a repeating pull, breathe, kick and glide cycle. The arms sweep out and back in a circle with the elbows high, then recover in front of the shoulders, while the legs bend, turn the feet out and snap back together. Underwater EMG of the kick shows adductor longus and adductor magnus peaking through leg retraction and the whip, with the abdominals joining as the legs flip, so this is the one stroke where the lower body carries most of the propulsion. Head and shoulders lift to breathe once each cycle.

For a catalog this clip covers the stroke most learn-to-swim and masters programs teach first. Use it in stroke-selection screens, timing explainers, and technique content on the kick.

name: Bulgarian Split Squat
tags: bulgarian split squat; single leg; leg exercise; glutes; bodyweight; lower body
benefits: Builds single-leg strength in the glutes, quads, and hamstrings.; Exposes and corrects left-right strength imbalances.; Improves hip stability and balance under load.
useCases: Single-leg accessory blocks in hypertrophy training apps; Athletic prep modules for sport performance platforms; Imbalance-correction tracks in rehab-adjacent content; Advanced leg-day programming for coaching apps
instructions: 1. Stand a stride-length away from a bench and place the top of your back foot on the bench behind you. ; 2. Square your hips forward and brace your core with your hands on your hips or at your chest. ; 3. Lower your back knee straight down toward the floor while keeping your front shin near vertical. ; 4. Drop until the back knee is just above the ground and the front thigh is roughly parallel to the floor. ; 5. Keep your weight in the front heel and your chest tall throughout the descent. ; 6. Drive through the front heel to push yourself back up, finishing with the front glute squeezed.
commonMistakes: Standing too close to the bench, which shoves the front knee too far forward and loads the joint.; Letting the front knee cave inward instead of tracking over the foot.; Pushing off the back foot instead of driving through the front heel — robs the front leg of work.; Twisting the hips to compensate for balance instead of staying square — kills the unilateral training.
shortDescription: A rear-foot-elevated split squat that punishes one leg at a time — the most effective single-leg builder in any program.
longDescription:
The Bulgarian split squat is the most effective single-leg exercise in lower-body training. By placing the back foot on a bench and sinking into a deep split-stance squat, it loads the front-leg glute and quad through a full range while exposing balance and hip stability gaps that bilateral squats hide. It is brutal, honest, and irreplaceable.

For app builders, this clip is essential inventory in any serious leg program — strength, hypertrophy, athletic prep, or rehab-adjacent training. It is the bridge between bilateral squats and true unilateral work, and it scales from bodyweight to heavy dumbbells or a barbell. Drop it into your library and it will appear in nearly every advanced leg-day template you ship.

name: Burpee
tags: burpee; hiit; conditioning; bodyweight; full body; cardio
benefits: Trains full-body strength and conditioning in a single movement.; Spikes the heart rate fast for efficient cardio work.; Builds explosive power, pressing strength, and core endurance at once.
useCases: HIIT and conditioning workout flows in fitness apps; CrossFit and hybrid training program assets; Bodyweight finisher modules for coaching platforms; High-engagement content for social fitness creators
instructions: 1. Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, arms relaxed at your sides, and core braced. ; 2. Drop into a low squat and place your hands on the floor just in front of your feet. ; 3. Kick or step both feet back so you land in a high plank position with arms straight. ; 4. Lower your chest to the floor in a controlled push-up, then press back up to the high plank. ; 5. Jump or step both feet back up under your hips into the squat position. ; 6. Explode upward into a jump with arms reaching overhead, land softly, and reset for the next rep.
commonMistakes: Skipping the push-up at the bottom and turning the burpee into a squat-thrust-jump instead.; Sagging the hips in the plank position, which strains the lower back over volume.; Landing the jump with stiff legs instead of absorbing softly into a quarter squat.; Going so fast that form collapses — turns a conditioning lift into a sloppy injury risk.
shortDescription: A squat-thrust into a push-up into a jump — the full-body conditioning move that hits everything in one rep.
longDescription:
The burpee is the most efficient full-body conditioning exercise ever programmed. In one rep, it chains a squat, a push-up, and a jump — training the chest, quads, core, and cardiovascular system in a single explosive sequence. It needs no equipment, scales endlessly, and gasses anyone in under a minute.

For app builders, the burpee is non-negotiable inventory in any HIIT, CrossFit, conditioning, or hybrid training library. It is also the most-searched bodyweight exercise on the internet, which makes the clip a strong organic-traffic asset for content and SEO pages. Ship it in your core library and it will live across dozens of workout templates and finisher modules.

name: Butterfly Swim
tags: butterfly; swimming; cardio; dolphin kick; advanced; pool
benefits: Loads back, chest and shoulders through the widest range of the four strokes.; Demands whole-body timing between the arm pull, kick and body wave.; Delivers the highest intensity of the competitive strokes for short efforts.
useCases: Advanced stroke libraries in swim and triathlon apps.; Stroke-comparison screens showing intensity ranking.; Technique modules on dolphin kick timing.; Muscle-highlight content for shoulder load education.
instructions: 1. Start prone with your body long and both arms extended in front of you. ; 2. Press both hands out and down together, keeping the elbows high. ; 3. Drive both arms back past your hips to finish the pull. ; 4. Sweep both arms over the water simultaneously into the next entry. ; 5. Beat both legs together in a dolphin kick timed to the entry and the finish. ; 6. Breathe forward once every second or third cycle as the arms clear the water.
commonMistakes: Lifting the head high to breathe, which sinks the hips and stalls the recovery.; Pulling with the arms only, so the body wave and kick stop contributing.; Mistiming the second kick, which leaves the arms to drag the body through the entry.; Swimming long sets while fatigued, exactly when shoulder mechanics start to break down.
shortDescription: Simultaneous double-arm swimming timed to a dolphin kick, with the body undulating around the hips through every cycle.
longDescription:
Butterfly moves both arms together: they enter overhead, pull through under the body and recover over the surface while the legs beat as one in a dolphin kick. Electromyographic analysis of twelve shoulder muscles found pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi generating the power through the pull, deltoids and rotator cuff controlling entry and recovery, and serratus anterior and subscapularis staying active throughout, so shoulder load runs continuously through the stroke cycle. The body teeter-totters around the hips, so the trunk works continuously to hold the rhythm.

For a catalog this is the hardest of the four strokes to film and the one most libraries lack. Use it in stroke-comparison screens, advanced swim sets, and technique content on timing.

name: Cable 30 Degree Shrug
tags: cable shrug; trap exercise; upper traps; cable machine; pull day; upper body
benefits: Builds upper-trap size along the natural fiber direction.; Develops back thickness and a stronger upper-back silhouette.; Trains the traps through a fuller range than standing dumbbell shrugs.
useCases: Pull-day accessory blocks in hypertrophy training apps; Trap-specialization modules for bodybuilding platforms; Form-teaching content for muscle-fiber education; Back-day finishers in coaching app program templates
instructions: 1. Set the cable at the lowest pulley setting and attach a straight bar or rope handle. ; 2. Stand a foot or two back from the cable and grip the handle with arms straight. ; 3. Lean your torso forward at about a 30-degree angle, keeping a flat back and braced core. ; 4. Let your shoulders relax forward and down so the cable pulls your traps into a stretch. ; 5. Shrug your shoulders up and slightly back along the angle of the cable, squeezing the traps hard. ; 6. Lower the weight back down under control over 2 to 3 seconds and repeat for high reps.
commonMistakes: Standing fully upright, which turns the lift into a regular straight-up shrug.; Bending the elbows instead of keeping the arms straight — loads the biceps, not the traps.; Rounding the lower back in the leaned-over position, which strains the spine over volume.; Using too much weight and rolling the shoulders forward instead of shrugging up and back.
shortDescription: A cable shrug performed at a 30-degree angle that loads the upper traps along their natural fiber line — the smarter shrug variation.
longDescription:
The cable 30 degree shrug is a shrug variation that loads the upper traps along the natural angle of their muscle fibers. By leaning slightly into a low pulley and shrugging up and back, it pulls the line of force away from straight vertical and into the diagonal that the upper traps actually run. The result is a stronger contraction and better trap development than a standard straight-up shrug.

For app builders, this clip is a smart inclusion in serious hypertrophy programs and pull-day accessory blocks where coaches want a more intentional trap exercise. It pairs well with rows and face pulls in pull-day finisher modules, and it is a useful teaching piece for explaining why fiber direction matters in muscle isolation.

name: Cable Bar Curl
tags: cable bar curl; biceps exercise; arm day; cable; isolation; upper body
benefits: Builds biceps size and peak with constant cable tension.; Trains both heads of the biceps through a full range of motion.; Reinforces strict elbow mechanics for cleaner curl form.
useCases: Arm-day finishers in strength training apps; Hypertrophy block accessories for coaching platforms; Pull-day program assets for online training tracks; Teaching clips for beginner curl-pattern modules
instructions: 1. Set the pulley to the lowest position and attach a straight bar, then grip it underhand at shoulder width. ; 2. Step back so the cable has tension at full arm extension and stand tall with your elbows tucked at your ribs. ; 3. Curl the bar up toward your shoulders by bending only at the elbows, keeping the upper arms locked in place. ; 4. Squeeze the biceps hard at the top with the bar a few inches from your collarbone. ; 5. Lower the bar slowly over 2 to 3 seconds, fighting the cable tension all the way back to full extension. ; 6. Reset your stance and repeat for 10 to 15 controlled reps without using your back or hips.
commonMistakes: Swinging the torso back to fling the bar up, which steals load from the biceps and risks lower-back strain.; Letting the elbows drift forward at the top, turning the curl into a partial front raise.; Cutting the lockout short at the bottom, missing the long-head stretch where most growth lives.; Rushing the lowering phase, which throws away the highest-tension half of the rep where the biceps grow most.
shortDescription: A two-handed cable curl using a straight bar attachment that hammers the biceps with constant tension from bottom to top.
longDescription:
The cable bar curl is a standing biceps exercise performed from a low cable pulley with a straight bar attachment. Unlike a barbell curl, the cable keeps tension on the biceps through the entire range of motion — there's no rest at the bottom and no slack at the top. It hits the long and short heads of the biceps evenly and is a staple of any arm-focused training block.

For app and content use, this clip slots cleanly into pull-day finishers, dedicated arm days, and hypertrophy-focused programs. It's also a clean teaching reference for beginners learning the curl pattern, since the cable enforces a clean elbow path and discourages body english. Pair it with pushdown clips for a full arm-day pairing in your library.

name: Cable Bar Face Pull
tags: cable bar face pull; rear delts; pull day; cable; shoulder health; upper body
benefits: Builds the rear delts and upper-back muscles that balance pressing work.; Reinforces healthy shoulder posture for desk workers and lifters alike.; Strengthens the small stabilizers around the shoulder blade for joint health.
useCases: Pull-day accessories in strength training apps; Postural-correction content for office-worker programs; Shoulder health modules in coaching platforms; Warm-up routines before heavy pressing in athletic prep apps
instructions: 1. Set the pulley above head height and attach a straight bar, then grip it overhand at shoulder width. ; 2. Step back until the cable has tension and stand with feet hip-width apart and a slight forward lean. ; 3. Pull the bar toward your forehead with the elbows flaring wide and high, leading with the back of the upper arms. ; 4. Squeeze your rear delts and upper back at the end of the pull, keeping your wrists in line with your forearms. ; 5. Slowly let the bar travel back to full arm extension over 2 to 3 seconds, keeping the chest tall. ; 6. Repeat for 12 to 20 reps, prioritizing the squeeze and elbow path over loading heavy weight.
commonMistakes: Pulling the bar too low toward the chin or chest, which turns the lift into a row and loses the rear-delt focus.; Letting the elbows drop instead of leading high and wide, swapping rear-delt work for biceps engagement.; Leaning back hard to use bodyweight as a counterweight instead of pulling cleanly with the back.; Loading too heavy and shrugging the traps up, hiding the rear delts under upper-trap dominance.
shortDescription: A high-cable face pull using a straight bar that targets the rear delts and upper-back posture muscles.
longDescription:
The cable bar face pull is a high-pulley pulling exercise performed with a straight bar. By pulling the bar toward the forehead with elbows high and wide, it isolates the rear delts and the upper-back muscles that hold the shoulders in healthy alignment. It's a key accessory for anyone who presses heavy and wants balanced shoulder development.

For app and content use, this clip belongs in any pull-day program, postural correction track, or shoulder health block. App builders shipping desk-worker or office-mobility content will get heavy reuse out of it. It also pairs well with rear-delt fly and reverse fly clips inside a dedicated shoulder accessories module.

name: Cable Bar Pushdown
tags: cable bar pushdown; triceps exercise; push day; cable; isolation; upper body
benefits: Builds triceps size and lockout strength with isolated tension.; Targets all three heads of the triceps through a full range of motion.; Reinforces stable elbow mechanics for stronger pressing lifts.
useCases: Push-day finishers in strength training apps; Arm-day program assets for hypertrophy tracks; Beginner triceps isolation modules in coaching platforms; Quick accessory clips for trainer Reels and TikToks
instructions: 1. Set the pulley to the highest position and attach a straight bar, then grip it overhand at shoulder width. ; 2. Step close to the stack and tuck your elbows tight against your ribs with your forearms parallel to the floor. ; 3. Press the bar straight down by extending your elbows fully, keeping the upper arms locked in place. ; 4. Squeeze the triceps hard at the bottom with the arms straight and the bar near your thighs. ; 5. Let the bar travel back up slowly over 2 seconds, stopping when your forearms are parallel to the floor. ; 6. Repeat for 10 to 15 reps, keeping a tall torso and avoiding any forward lean to muscle the bar down.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare forward and away from the ribs, turning the lift into a chest-driven press.; Leaning the torso forward to push down with bodyweight, which steals load from the triceps.; Cutting the lockout short, missing the strongest contraction at the bottom of the movement.; Bouncing the weight up at the top instead of controlling the return, throwing away half the working set.
shortDescription: A standing triceps pushdown using a straight bar attachment — the most efficient way to isolate the triceps with cables.
longDescription:
The cable bar pushdown is a standing single-joint triceps exercise performed from a high pulley. With the elbows pinned to the ribs, you press a straight bar down to lockout, isolating the triceps with constant cable tension. It's one of the most efficient ways to overload the triceps without involving the shoulders or chest.

For app and content use, this clip is a recognizable inclusion in any push-day finisher or arm-focused training block. It pairs naturally with cable curl clips for a paired-set arm day in your library, and it serves as a clean teaching piece for beginners learning to lock out the elbow under load.

name: Cable Bench Chest Fly
tags: cable bench chest fly; chest exercise; push day; cable; isolation; upper body
benefits: Builds chest size with constant cable tension through a full arc.; Develops the inner-chest squeeze that pressing alone misses.; Trains the chest in deep stretch for stronger hypertrophy stimulus.
useCases: Hypertrophy chest blocks in coaching platforms; Push-day accessories in fitness apps; Mind-muscle education modules for beginners; Aesthetic-focused content for chest-development tracks
instructions: 1. Position a flat bench between two cable stations and set both pulleys to the lowest position with single handles. ; 2. Lie back on the bench and press both handles up over your chest with a slight bend in your elbows. ; 3. Lower the handles out to your sides in a wide arc, keeping the elbow angle locked the whole way down. ; 4. Stop when your hands are roughly level with your shoulders and you feel a deep stretch across the chest. ; 5. Bring the handles back together in the same arc by squeezing the chest, finishing with the hands meeting above you. ; 6. Pause at the top with a hard chest squeeze, then repeat for 10 to 15 controlled reps.
commonMistakes: Bending the elbows mid-rep, which turns the fly into a sloppy press and shifts load off the chest.; Dropping the hands too far below shoulder level, overstretching the front shoulders and risking joint strain.; Rushing the lowering phase, where most of the chest-building tension lives.; Letting the shoulders roll forward off the bench, losing the stable platform that keeps the chest loaded.
shortDescription: A bench-supported cable fly that puts the chest under deep stretch with constant tension top to bottom.
longDescription:
The cable bench chest fly is a single-joint chest exercise performed lying on a flat bench between two cable pulleys. By hugging the arms together in an arc, it isolates the chest with constant cable tension — and unlike a dumbbell fly, the resistance doesn't fall off as the hands meet at the top. The bench keeps the upper back stable so the chest can do all the work.

For app and content use, this clip is a strong fit for hypertrophy chest blocks, dedicated push days, and accessory work after heavy pressing. It's also a clean teaching piece for showing how to feel the chest contracting in isolation, which makes it valuable in beginner mind-muscle education modules and trainer-led content.

name: Cable Bench Press
tags: cable bench press; chest exercise; push day; cable; horizontal press; upper body
benefits: Builds chest and triceps strength with smooth, constant tension.; Removes the lockout dead spot found in barbell pressing.; Allows independent arm work to expose and fix side-to-side imbalances.
useCases: Push-day workout flows in strength training apps; Hypertrophy chest variations for coaching platforms; Cable-machine-focused programs for commercial-gym users; Alternative pressing modules in beginner-friendly tracks
instructions: 1. Place a flat bench between two cable stations and set both pulleys to the lowest position with single handles. ; 2. Lie back on the bench and press both handles up so your arms are extended directly over your chest. ; 3. Lower the handles to chest level with the elbows tracking at about 60 to 75 degrees from your torso. ; 4. Pause briefly at the bottom with a deep chest stretch and a tight upper back pressed into the bench. ; 5. Press both handles back up in a slight arc until they meet above your chest at full arm extension. ; 6. Squeeze the chest at the top and repeat for 8 to 12 controlled reps.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare wide to 90 degrees, which strains the front shoulders and reduces chest engagement.; Pressing the handles in different paths, causing one side to dominate and creating uneven loading.; Cutting the lockout short, missing the chest-squeeze position at the top of the press.; Lifting the head or hips off the bench for leverage, which destabilizes the press.
shortDescription: A bench-supported cable press that trains the chest and triceps with smooth, constant tension through the full press.
longDescription:
The cable bench press is a horizontal pressing exercise performed lying on a flat bench between two low cable pulleys. It trains the chest and triceps in the same pattern as a barbell or dumbbell bench press, but with a key difference — cable tension stays steady through the entire range, with no dead spot at the lockout. That makes it a strong hypertrophy variation for lifters who want a different stimulus than a barbell or dumbbell press.

For app and content use, this clip fits cleanly into any push-day program and gives a clear alternative to barbell pressing for users who train at cable-heavy commercial gyms. It pairs well with cable fly clips inside a chest-focused hypertrophy block and gives coaches a fresh angle for variety in long-running programs.

name: Cable Bench Straight Leg Kickback
tags: cable kickback; glute exercise; leg day; cable; isolation; lower body
benefits: Isolates and builds the glutes without involving the quads.; Strengthens hip extension for sport, sprinting, and heavier hinges.; Shapes the glutes from a different angle than squats and deadlifts.
useCases: Glute-day programming in fitness apps; Lower-body hypertrophy blocks in coaching platforms; Shape-focused training tracks for women's fitness apps; Warm-up flows before heavy hinge work in athletic prep
instructions: 1. Attach a cable cuff to your ankle and set the pulley to the lowest position, then face the cable stack. ; 2. Stand a few feet back from the stack and rest your forearms on a flat bench in front of you. ; 3. Brace your core and start with the working leg lightly forward so the cable has tension at rest. ; 4. Drive the straight leg back and up by squeezing the glute, finishing in line with or slightly above your torso. ; 5. Pause at the top for a hard glute squeeze, keeping your hips level and your lower back neutral. ; 6. Lower the leg under control back to the start, then repeat for 12 to 15 reps before switching sides.
commonMistakes: Arching the lower back to throw the leg higher, which loads the spine instead of the glutes.; Letting the working hip rotate open, which lets the lower back take over the movement.; Bending the knee mid-rep, swapping glute work for hamstring engagement.; Rushing the return phase and letting the cable yank the leg forward instead of controlling the descent.
shortDescription: A bench-supported cable kickback that isolates the glutes with a straight-leg drive against constant cable tension.
longDescription:

longDescription:
Cable external rotation loads the infraspinatus and teres minor through the range they actually control, turning the upper arm outward. The pulley sits at about waist height and the lifter stands side on, so the cable pulls across the body and resistance stays constant from start to finish. The working elbow is pinned to the ribs and bent to ninety degrees; the forearm sweeps outward until the cable has passed in front of the stomach. Loads stay light because the rotators are small and the leverage is poor by design.

As catalog inventory this clip pairs naturally with the banded version for equipment-filtered browsing. It slots into shoulder warm-up sequences, cable machine collections, and prehab modules where a constant-tension option is preferred over an elastic one.

The cable front raise is a front raise fed from a low pulley instead of a dumbbell. You stand facing away from the stack with the cable running between your legs, take the handle in both hands with an overhand grip, and raise your arms straight in front of you to shoulder height. The front deltoids are the target with the traps and upper back assisting, and the cable holds tension steady across the range instead of falling away at the bottom as a dumbbell does. The shoulder flexion path is simple enough that the movement suits beginners.

For a library this is the constant-tension member of the front raise family. It belongs in cable equipment filters, shoulder accessory blocks, and content comparing cable, dumbbell and plate front raises.

longDescription:
The cable high-to-low fly is a single-joint chest movement performed between two pulleys set at their highest position. You keep the elbows fixed and slightly bent, moving only at the shoulder until both hands meet in front of the hips. That downward adduction path emphasizes the lower, sternal region of the pectoralis major, with the front deltoid and triceps assisting.

Because the resistance pulls from above, tension stays on the chest across the whole arc instead of dropping off near the top the way a dumbbell fly does.

As an asset this is the default lower-chest isolation clip: it fills cable equipment filters, chest accessory slots and push-day builders that need a fly angle distinct from the flat and low-to-high versions.

Cable hip abduction isolates the muscles that move the leg away from the midline. An ankle strap on a low pulley loads the outside leg, and you lift it sideways with the knee straight, leading with the heel so the gluteus medius and minimus do the work rather than the hip flexors. Those muscles hold the pelvis level during single leg movements such as walking, running and stair climbing, which is why they are trained deliberately. The standing leg and the abdominals stabilize the trunk against the pull of the cable.

For a library this is the cleanest demonstration of hip abduction available and pairs with band and machine versions of the same pattern. It fits cable machine filters, glute accessory blocks, and prehab or running specific content where lateral hip strength is the point.

The cable incline bench press is an upper-chest pressing exercise performed on an incline bench between two low cable pulleys. It's one of the most reliable ways to build the upper-chest shelf that gives a chest its full, finished look.

For app and content use, this clip is a high-impact addition to any hypertrophy chest block or aesthetic-driven push-day program. It's especially valuable in physique-focused training tracks where upper-chest development drives the look. The cable kickback fastens an ankle cuff to a low pulley and drives one leg back behind you while the torso stays still. Because the cable pulls forward from floor level, the gluteus maximus has to finish hip extension against tension that never drops off. The hamstrings assist at the hip and the abs brace so the range comes from the hip rather than the lower back. Quadruped hip extension ranks among the highest gluteus maximus activation patterns tested, and this is the standing, cable-loaded form of that same joint action.

In a library this is the glute isolation clip for cable equipped gyms. It fits glute focused program blocks, accessory work after squats or hinges, and single leg symmetry work in rehab oriented app content.

You stand side-on to the stack with the working arm furthest from it, reach across your body for the handle, then raise the arm out to the side until it is level with the floor. The single-arm cable version stays beginner-level as long as the chest is tall and the hips stay level, and the cable holds constant tension through the arc. A trial comparing dumbbell and cable lateral raises over eight weeks found both grew the lateral deltoid by a similar amount.

In a catalog this covers unilateral side-delt work on a cable stack, which most libraries carry only as a two-arm dumbbell raise. Use it in cable filters, unilateral accessory blocks, and resistance-profile comparison content.

Elbows stay slightly bent and fixed, so the only joint working is the shoulder, and the upward arc shifts emphasis toward the upper, clavicular region of the pectoralis major. The front deltoid assists more here than in a downward fly.

Trunk control decides whether the work stays in the chest. A staggered stance and braced abdominals stop the movement turning into a leaning shoulder raise.

In a catalog this clip is the upper-chest cable asset that pairs with the high-to-low version, giving app and program builders a complete cable fly set for chest filters and accessory blocks.

The cable overhead press is a standing vertical pressing exercise performed from two low cable pulleys. By pressing the handles from shoulder height to full lockout overhead, it trains the front and side shoulders along with the triceps under constant cable tension. The standing setup also forces the core and glutes to brace hard against the load, making it as much a full-body lift as a shoulder lift.

For app and content use, this clip fits cleanly into push-day programs, dedicated shoulder days, and strength-focused training blocks. It's also a strong fit for athletic-prep tracks where standing overhead pressing patterns transfer to throwing, blocking, and overhead sport movements. The cable pec fly is a standing single-joint chest exercise performed between two chest-height cable pulleys. By hugging the arms together in a wide arc, it isolates the chest and removes the help that triceps and front shoulders give during pressing lifts. The cable keeps tension constant — there's no rest at the top, and the deep stretch at the bottom is one of the strongest hypertrophy positions you can train.

For app and content use, this clip is a clean fit for hypertrophy chest blocks, push-day finishers, and aesthetic-driven training programs. It's also a strong teaching piece for showing the chest contracting in isolation, which makes it valuable in mind-muscle education modules and trainer-led short-form content.

The cable pull through is a hip hinge where the resistance comes from behind rather than from a bar on the back. A rope on the lowest pulley is held between the legs, and the lifter hinges until the torso is close to parallel before driving the hips forward to stand. Because the load line runs horizontally, the spine carries very little compressive force while the glutes and hamstrings still work through a full range. That combination makes it a common teaching tool for the hinge pattern and a high-volume glute exercise when heavier hinging is fatiguing.

As an asset this clip is worth its place in any glute or posterior chain collection. It supports hinge-teaching sequences in app programs, cable machine equipment pages, and low back friendly alternatives inside programming decision trees.

The cable rope hammer curl keeps the palms facing each other on a rope attached to a low pulley, so the elbow flexes with the forearm in a neutral position. The cable keeps tension on the arm at the bottom of the rep, where a dumbbell hammer curl unloads completely, and the elbows stay pinned to your sides so the shoulders cannot swing the weight up.

For a library this is the neutral grip arm clip that pairs with a supinated cable curl. It works in arm day accessory blocks, grip and forearm focused programming, and side by side content explaining how grip changes elbow flexor recruitment.

benefits: Isolates wrist flexion, which most pulling exercises never train directly.; Builds the forearm flexors that close the grip on bars and handles.; Cable tension stays even across a very short range of motion.
useCases: Grip and forearm accessory blocks in a training app.; Climbing, racket sport and combat sport program tracks.; Elbow and wrist rehab content in coaching platforms.; Forearm filtered library entries in an exercise browser.
instructions: 1. Attach a straight bar to a low pulley and set a light weight. ; 2. Sit on a bench facing the stack with your feet about shoulder width apart. ; 3. Grip the bar underhand at shoulder width and rest your elbows on your inner thighs. ; 4. Let the bar drop by bending only at the wrists, allowing it to roll toward your fingers. ; 5. Close your grip and curl your wrists upward, squeezing the forearms at the top. ; 6. Pause briefly, then lower under control and repeat for reps.
commonMistakes: Loading too heavy, which turns the rep into an elbow curl and hides the wrist range.; Lifting the elbows off the thighs, so the forearms move and the wrists stay locked.; Skipping the roll to the fingers, which leaves out the grip closing part of the movement.; Bouncing at the bottom, which loads the wrist joint rather than the flexors.
shortDescription: Seated cable wrist curl with the forearms braced that isolates wrist flexion and builds grip strength.
longDescription:
The cable wrist curl braces the forearms against the thighs or a bench with a bar held underhand from a low pulley, so the only joint that moves is the wrist. Letting the bar roll toward the fingertips at the bottom and then closing the hand and flexing the wrist trains the forearm flexors that both bend the wrist and shut the grip. The cable holds a steady pull at every point in that short travel, which matters because the range itself is only a few inches. Light weight and a deliberate pause at the top do far more here than heavy loading.

For a library this is the dedicated forearm clip most catalogs skip. It fits grip and forearm accessory blocks, climbing and racket sport programs, and elbow rehab content where controlled wrist flexion is the whole point.

name: Captain's Chair Knee Raise
tags: knee raise; captains chair; abs; core; hanging; gym station
benefits: Ranked first for oblique activation and second for rectus abdominis activation in electromyography testing across thirteen abdominal movements.; Supports the back and forearms, so grip strength does not limit the set the way it does when hanging from a bar.; Progresses simply by moving from bent knees to straight legs without changing the setup.
useCases: Gym-floor core option in app builders that can assume station access.; Power tower and captain's chair station onboarding content.; Evidence-led editorial comparing abdominal exercise effectiveness.; Progression ladders that lead from knee raises to straight leg raises.
instructions: 1. Step into a captain's chair station and place your forearms on the pads with your back against the rest. ; 2. Grip the handles, let your legs hang straight down and take the weight off your feet. ; 3. Brace your abdominals and press your lower back lightly into the pad. ; 4. Raise both knees toward your chest, finishing the rep by curling the pelvis upward. ; 5. Pause at the top with the abdominals fully shortened. ; 6. Lower the legs slowly back to a straight hang and repeat without swinging.
commonMistakes: Swinging the legs up with momentum, which lets the hip flexors do the work the abdominals should do.; Stopping at hip height without tilting the pelvis, which leaves the rectus abdominis barely loaded.; Dropping the legs at the end of the rep, which throws away the eccentric and stresses the low back.; Shrugging into the shoulder pads, which loads the neck and traps instead of the trunk.
shortDescription: A supported hanging knee raise from a captain's chair station, curling the pelvis to load the abdominals directly.
longDescription:
The captain's chair knee raise is performed in a padded upright station with the forearms on the pads and the back against the rest, so the trunk is supported and the legs hang free. Raising the knees toward the chest flexes the hips, and finishing the rep by curling the pelvis is what shifts the work from the hip flexors onto the abdominals. Electromyography testing across thirteen abdominal exercises ranked the captain's chair first for oblique activation and second for rectus abdominis activation.

For a product catalog this clip covers a gym-floor movement that home-only libraries miss. It fits abdominal blocks in app programs, power tower onboarding content, and editorial comparing abdominal exercises.

name: Chest-Supported Dumbbell Row
tags: dumbbell row; chest supported; back; upper back; incline bench; horizontal pull
benefits: Rows heavy loads without stressing the lower back.; Chest support removes momentum so each rep stays strict.; Neutral grip is comfortable for shoulders and wrists.
useCases: Back hypertrophy blocks that need high rep volume without spinal fatigue.; Lower back friendly swap when a bent over row is off the table.; Paired pulling clip for incline press supersets.; Beginner rowing option that stays safe to coach remotely.
instructions: 1. Set an adjustable bench to roughly 45 degrees and pick up two dumbbells. ; 2. Lie face down on the pad with your chest supported and your arms hanging. ; 3. Hold the dumbbells with palms facing each other and neutral wrists. ; 4. Retract your shoulder blades and pull your elbows behind your body. ; 5. Stop when your elbows reach or just pass the line of your torso. ; 6. Lower the dumbbells slowly to full arm extension and repeat.
commonMistakes: Peeling the chest off the pad to add range, which reintroduces the back extension you removed.; Swinging the dumbbells up, so the pull comes from momentum rather than muscle.; Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears instead of retracting the blades.; Squeezing the handles hard with a full grip, which lets the biceps take over the pull.
shortDescription: A prone incline dumbbell row that removes the hinge so the mid back and lats work without lower back load.
longDescription:
Lying face down on a bench set near 45 degrees takes the hip hinge and the spinal bracing out of a dumbbell row. From a neutral grip with the dumbbells hanging, you retract the shoulder blades and drive the elbows behind the torso until they reach or just pass the midline. Because the chest is fixed against the pad, momentum is hard to generate, so the mid trapezius, rhomboids and lats absorb the load while the biceps and rear delts assist.

This clip is useful anywhere lower back load is a constraint: rehab-adjacent programs, high-volume hypertrophy blocks, and beginner flows where a free bent over row is still too demanding to coach remotely. It also fits dumbbell-only equipment filters, and it works well as the paired row in an incline press superset inside an app.

name: Chest-Supported T-Bar Row
tags: t-bar row; chest supported; machine row; back; upper back; horizontal pull
benefits: Strict heavy rowing with no hinge or bracing requirement.; Fixed path keeps the elbow line consistent rep to rep.; Neutral and overhand grips both train the mid back.
useCases: Machine filter for commercial gyms that own a chest-supported row station.; Heavy row slot in back day templates.; Exercise swap list for members avoiding spinal loading.; Form-cue overlay content on elbow path and scapular retraction.
instructions: 1. Load plates onto the T-bar row post and set the chest pad height. ; 2. Lie chest down on the pad with your feet flat on the platform. ; 3. Take the handles with a neutral or overhand grip and straighten your arms. ; 4. Brace your abdominals and pull your shoulder blades together. ; 5. Row the handles back until your elbows pass the line of your torso. ; 6. Lower the load under control to a full stretch and repeat.
commonMistakes: Pushing the chest off the pad to finish the rep, which loads the lumbar spine.; Cutting the range short at the bottom, so the lats never reach full stretch.; Leading with the hands instead of the elbows, which shifts work to the biceps.; Choosing a load that forces jerky partial reps, which trains momentum not the back.
shortDescription: A plate-loaded T-bar row taken from a prone chest pad, so the mid back and lats pull without a free hinge.
longDescription:
The chest supported T-bar row fixes your torso against an angled pad while the loading arm travels on a single pivot. You take a neutral or pronated grip, retract the shoulder blades and drive the elbows behind the body until they reach or pass the torso line, then lower to full extension. The pad removes the isometric hinge demand of a free-standing T-bar row, so here the latissimus dorsi, mid trapezius and rhomboids handle the load with the biceps and rear delts assisting.

For an asset library this is the machine counterpart to the chest supported dumbbell row and it covers a station most commercial gyms have. It fits machine equipment filters, back day templates that need one strict heavy row, and swap lists for members who should not load a hinge.

name: Chin Ups
tags: chin ups; vertical pull; back exercise; biceps; bodyweight; pull day
benefits: Builds the lats, biceps, and grip with one bodyweight movement.; Develops relative strength that transfers to climbing, sport, and lifting.; Trains the vertical pull pattern that balances out pressing work.
useCases: Pull-day workout flows in strength training apps; Calisthenics and bodyweight program tracks; Beginner-to-advanced upper-body progression modules; Hero clips for back, biceps, and pull-up content
instructions: 1. Reach up and grip the bar with palms facing you, hands about shoulder-width apart. ; 2. Hang at full arm extension with the shoulders pulled down away from the ears and the core braced. ; 3. Pull yourself up by driving the elbows down toward your ribs, leading with the chest. ; 4. Continue the pull until your chin clears the bar and your upper chest is close to the bar. ; 5. Pause for a beat at the top, squeezing the back and biceps without swinging. ; 6. Lower yourself slowly to a full hang over 2 to 3 seconds, then repeat for reps.
commonMistakes: Kipping or swinging the legs to generate momentum instead of pulling cleanly with the back and arms.; Cutting the range short by stopping before the chin clears the bar or skipping the full hang at the bottom.; Shrugging the shoulders up at the start so the traps take over and the lats never engage.; Dropping fast at the bottom and skipping the slow lowering phase, where most of the strength gains happen.
shortDescription: A vertical bodyweight pull with palms facing you that builds the lats, biceps, and grip in one of the most honest strength tests there is.
longDescription:
The chin up is the benchmark vertical pulling exercise. With an underhand grip, you pull your full bodyweight up until your chin clears the bar — loading the lats heavily while bringing the biceps in as a major mover. It's one of the cleanest tests of relative upper-body strength in any program.

This clip earns a permanent spot in any strength app's core library. It's the natural pair to the bench press on any push-and-pull split, and it shows up in calisthenics, beginner-strength, and athletic-prep programs alike. App builders and creators can use it as a hero clip for back content where a generic lat pulldown wouldn't carry the same weight.

name: Close-Grip Barbell Curl
tags: close grip barbell curl; barbell curl; biceps; forearms; isolation; grip width
benefits: Trains elbow flexion with a fixed grip width that is easy to repeat session to session.; The narrow grip shifts emphasis toward the outer part of the biceps.; A bar allows small load jumps, so progression is simple to track.
useCases: Arm day templates in a strength training app.; Barbell-only program tracks for home gyms.; Grip width comparison content for coaches.; Barbell filtered library entries in an exercise browser.
instructions: 1. Load a straight barbell and stand with your feet about hip width apart. ; 2. Take an underhand grip with your hands inside shoulder width. ; 3. Stand tall with the bar at arms length and your elbows at your sides. ; 4. Brace your abs and curl the bar toward your shoulders. ; 5. Squeeze the biceps at the top without letting the elbows travel forward. ; 6. Lower under control, stopping just short of a locked elbow, then repeat.
commonMistakes: Swinging the hips to start the bar moving, which takes load off the biceps.; Letting the elbows drift back behind the torso, which shortens the working range.; Gripping so narrow that the wrists ache, which limits load before the biceps are trained.; Dropping the bar quickly, which skips the eccentric where much of the stimulus sits.
shortDescription: Standing barbell curl with the hands set inside shoulder width, shifting emphasis toward the outer biceps.
longDescription:
The close-grip barbell curl loads a straight bar with the hands narrower than shoulder width and the palms facing up. Narrowing the grip rotates the upper arms slightly outward, and the standard coaching claim is that it biases the outer or long head of the biceps compared with a wide grip. Both heads still work, so treat the difference as a shift in emphasis rather than a separate exercise. Keep the elbows pinned at your sides, stop the chest and hips helping, and hold a small bend at the bottom so tension never fully leaves the arm.

As an asset this covers the grip width variation of the barbell curl that libraries usually reduce to a single clip. It fits arm day templates, progressive overload tracks built around a bar, and side by side content on how grip width changes a curl.

name: Cossack Squat
tags: cossack squat; lateral squat; adductors; hip mobility; bodyweight; frontal plane
benefits: Trains strength in the frontal plane that forward facing leg work misses.; Loads the adductors and hamstrings of the extended leg through a long stretch.; Builds hip, knee and ankle range that carries over to every squat pattern.
useCases: Bodyweight and mobility programs in a fitness app.; Warm up flows before heavy squat and lunge sessions.; Athletic preparation content for lateral movement sports.; Frontal plane filter examples in a movement pattern browser.
instructions: 1. Stand with your feet well outside shoulder width and toes pointing forward. ; 2. Brace your abdominals and lift your chest tall. ; 3. Shift your weight over one leg and bend that knee, sitting the hips back and down. ; 4. Keep the other leg straight and let its foot roll onto the heel with the toes up. ; 5. Descend only as far as your hips and ankles allow with the loaded heel flat. ; 6. Push through the bent leg to return to center, then repeat on the other side.
commonMistakes: Arching the lower back to reach depth, which loads the lumbar spine instead of the hips.; Letting the heel of the squatting leg lift, which is an ankle mobility limit, not a strength one.; Bending the extended leg, which removes the adductor and hamstring stretch.; Rushing the transition between sides, which loses control at the deepest position.
shortDescription: A deep sideways squat on one leg with the other leg extended straight, worked in the frontal plane.
longDescription:
The Cossack squat takes a wide stance and shifts the whole body over one leg. That leg goes into deep hip, knee and ankle flexion while the other stays straight with the foot rolled onto its heel, which puts the inner thigh and hamstring of the extended leg under a long stretch. Because the movement runs side to side rather than front to back, it trains the frontal plane that most leg exercises leave alone. It demands real hip, knee and ankle range, so depth should follow available mobility rather than being forced.

For a library this is the frontal plane strength and mobility clip that squats and lunges do not cover. It fits bodyweight programs, warm up and mobility flows, and athletic prep content where lateral hip range and adductor strength are the goal.

name: Cross-Body Hammer Curl
tags: cross body hammer curl; pinwheel curl; dumbbell curl; biceps; brachialis; forearms
benefits: Neutral grip loads the brachialis and brachioradialis alongside the biceps.; One arm at a time makes side to side rep and load matching simple.; Needs only a pair of dumbbells, so it fits home and hotel gym programs.
useCases: Dumbbell-only program tracks in a training app.; Forearm and elbow flexor accessory blocks.; Short form demo content for home workout apps.; Brachialis emphasis in arm phases that rotate curl angles from week to week.
instructions: 1. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with your palms facing your body. ; 2. Stand tall with your feet hip width apart and your abs braced. ; 3. Keep a small bend in the elbows and set your shoulders back and down. ; 4. Curl one dumbbell diagonally across your chest toward the opposite shoulder. ; 5. Squeeze at the top without letting the dumbbell touch your body. ; 6. Lower under control to your side, then repeat with the other arm.
commonMistakes: Resting the dumbbell against the chest at the top, which unloads the arm mid rep.; Rotating the torso to meet the dumbbell, which shortens the range the arm actually works.; Letting the elbow swing forward, so the front of the shoulder lifts the weight.; Shrugging the shoulder up as the dumbbell rises, which moves work to the traps.
shortDescription: Dumbbell hammer curl swept diagonally across the torso, loading the biceps, brachialis and forearms.
longDescription:
The cross-body hammer curl, also called the pinwheel curl, holds a dumbbell with a neutral grip and curls it diagonally across the body toward the opposite shoulder. The neutral wrist keeps the brachialis and brachioradialis heavily involved alongside the biceps brachii, and the diagonal path keeps the dumbbell off the torso so the arm controls the weight instead of resting it. You work one arm at a time, which slows the set down and makes matching reps side to side straightforward. Keep the elbow close to your ribs and the shoulder still so the arm does the moving.

In a library this is the neutral grip dumbbell clip that pairs with a standard hammer curl. It works in dumbbell-only program tracks, forearm and elbow flexor accessory blocks, and short demo content for home training apps.

name: Cuban Press
tags: cuban press; dumbbell; rotator cuff; shoulders; external rotation; prehab
benefits: Loads the rotator cuff in a rotated overhead position that most pressing movements do not reach.; Combines mobility and strength work in a single rep, which saves warm-up time.; Exposes shoulder mobility restrictions early, before heavier pressing is loaded.
useCases: Shoulder prehab and warm-up blocks in dumbbell training programs.; Rotator cuff education content for coaching platforms.; Advanced shoulder accessory slots in app program builders.; Overhead athlete preparation content for swimming, throwing and racket sport programs.
instructions: 1. Stand tall with a light dumbbell in each hand, palms facing your thighs. ; 2. Set your shoulder blades down and back and brace your trunk. ; 3. Pull the dumbbells up the front of your body until the upper arms are parallel to the floor. ; 4. Holding the elbows at that height, rotate the forearms up and back into a goalpost position. ; 5. Press the dumbbells overhead until the arms are almost straight. ; 6. Reverse the three phases in order and return to the start under control.
commonMistakes: Loading it like a shoulder press, which makes the rotation phase impossible to control.; Letting the elbows drop during the rotation, which removes the external rotation the exercise exists for.; Arching the lower back to finish the press, which hides limited overhead mobility.; Rushing the sequence, which blends the three phases and loses the cuff work entirely.
shortDescription: A three-phase dumbbell drill that links an upright row, an external rotation and an overhead press in one rep.
longDescription:
The Cuban press chains three movements together. Light dumbbells are pulled up the front of the body into an upright row, the forearms then rotate up and back into a goalpost position, and the press finishes overhead. The rotation phase is the point of the exercise: it loads the external rotators of the cuff in a position most pressing does not reach, which is why it is normally trained with light loads. Deltoids and traps carry the row and the press, and the triceps finish the lockout.

For an asset library this clip covers a shoulder health movement that is hard to teach from a static image because the sequence matters more than any single position. It fits shoulder prehab blocks, warm-up sequences in dumbbell programs, and educational content on rotator cuff loading.

name: Cycling Cooldown
tags: cycling; cooldown; stretch; adductors; flexibility; recovery
benefits: Restores inner-thigh and hamstring range after repetitive hip flexion on the bike.; Needs no equipment, so it fits any post-ride setting.; Gives a clear, timed hold that is easy to program and coach.
useCases: Post-ride cool-down blocks in a cycling app.; Static-hold entries carrying a timed fifteen to thirty second prescription.; Recovery-day sequences for riders after long saddle time.; Adductor and hamstring flexibility content for coaches.
instructions: 1. Sit upright on the floor and open your legs into a comfortable wide straddle. ; 2. Extend both knees and point your toes toward the ceiling. ; 3. Brace your abdominal muscles to stabilize your spine and exhale slowly. ; 4. Hinge forward from the hips, reaching your hands ahead and keeping a flat back. ; 5. Stop at the point of tension and hold for fifteen to thirty seconds without bouncing. ; 6. Return to upright, rest briefly, then repeat the hold two to four times.
commonMistakes: Rounding the lower back to reach further, which shifts strain onto the spine.; Bouncing into the stretch instead of holding it, which triggers a protective contraction.; Letting the knees roll in and the toes drop, which takes tension off the adductors.; Pushing to pain rather than tension, which is how groin strains are aggravated.
shortDescription: Seated wide-leg forward stretch used after riding, opening the inner thighs with the hamstrings and calves along for it.
longDescription:
This clip shows a seated straddle stretch, the static hold most riders use once they are off the bike. You sit with the legs wide, knees extended and toes pointing up, brace the trunk, then hinge forward from the hips with a flat back until you feel tension through the inner thighs. The stretch also reaches the hamstrings, calves and back. Guidance is to hold fifteen to thirty seconds and repeat two to four times, moving from the hips rather than rounding the lower back, and never bouncing into range.

For a catalog this is a cool-down and flexibility asset rather than a cardio one. Use it in post-ride recovery blocks, mobility screens for cyclists, and adductor-focused stretching sequences.

name: Cycling Intervals
tags: cycling; intervals; cardio; quads; endurance; bike
benefits: Improves ventilatory threshold within a small number of sessions.; Keeps a low-impact pattern while intensity climbs.; Uses a repeatable structure that is easy to prescribe and track.
useCases: Interval timer screens in a cycling or endurance app.; Structured indoor training plans built around effort blocks.; Program builders that need a repeatable cardio unit.; Progress content comparing effort levels on the same clip.
instructions: 1. Set saddle height so your knee stays slightly bent at the bottom of the stroke. ; 2. Ride easy for several minutes until your breathing and cadence settle. ; 3. Hold a stable seated position with relaxed shoulders and a light grip. ; 4. Lift effort to the target for the work interval without changing your position. ; 5. Drop back to easy pedalling for the full recovery before the next effort. ; 6. Repeat the work and recovery pattern, then ride easy to finish.
commonMistakes: Starting the first effort too hard, so the last intervals collapse.; Cutting recovery short, which turns the session into one long moderate ride.; Rocking the hips at high effort instead of driving through the pedals.; Raising cadence without resistance, so effort never reaches the target.
shortDescription: Seated cycling run as repeated hard efforts with recoveries between them, holding a stable position throughout.
longDescription:
Interval riding keeps the pedalling pattern constant and varies only the effort. The quadriceps are the muscles that separate hard riding from easy riding: EMG work across eight lower-limb muscles found the vastus medialis, vastus lateralis and rectus femoris responding most to changes in pedalling demand, with glutes, hamstrings and calves supporting the stroke. A standard laboratory protocol is four thirty-second efforts against a fixed load with four minutes of recovery, repeated six times over two weeks, which is enough to move ventilatory threshold by roughly fifteen percent.

For a catalog this clip is the workhorse of structured cycling content. Use it in interval timer screens, indoor training plans, and program builders that need a repeatable effort block.

name: Cycling Sprint
tags: cycling; sprint; cardio; quads; hiit; bike
benefits: Raises ventilatory threshold in as few as six sessions.; Delivers maximal intensity without impact on the joints.; Produces a clean, measurable output for testing and pacing.
useCases: Sprint interval timer screens in an endurance app.; Fitness testing flows built on repeatable maximal efforts.; Conditioning blocks that need a maximal low-impact option.; Coaching content contrasting sprint and steady riding.
instructions: 1. Warm up with several minutes of easy riding before attempting any sprint. ; 2. Select a resistance heavy enough that cadence cannot run away from you. ; 3. Settle into a stable seated position with a firm grip on the bars. ; 4. Accelerate to maximum effort within the first few pedal strokes. ; 5. Hold peak output for the full sprint window without shifting position. ; 6. Spin easy for several minutes of recovery before the next sprint.
commonMistakes: Sprinting against too little resistance, so cadence spikes and force stays low.; Building up gradually, which wastes most of a thirty-second window.; Shortening recovery, which caps the output of every subsequent sprint.; Sprinting cold, which is when hamstring and knee complaints appear.
shortDescription: Maximal short cycling efforts where output peaks in seconds and the quads carry the load through every pedal stroke.
longDescription:
A cycling sprint is an all-out effort measured in seconds rather than minutes. The reference protocol is thirty seconds against a load set to seven and a half percent of bodyweight, with four minutes of recovery between repeats. Six such sessions across two weeks raised ventilatory threshold by around fifteen percent without changing peak oxygen uptake, so sprints buy threshold and anaerobic capacity rather than aerobic ceiling. Mechanically nothing changes from steady riding except force: the quadriceps group drives the stroke while glutes, hamstrings and calves support it.

For a catalog this clip is the high-intensity end of the cycling set. Use it in sprint interval timers, testing screens, and conditioning blocks that need a maximal low-impact option.

name: Cycling Warmup
tags: cycling; warmup; mobility; dynamic; hip; movement prep
benefits: Takes the hip through a range that pedalling never reaches.; Raises tissue temperature, which improves rapid force production.; Needs no equipment and fits in a few minutes before a session.
useCases: Pre-ride warm-up sequences in a cycling app.; Movement prep libraries for coaches and class instructors.; Mobility screens paired with the post-ride stretch clip.; Onboarding flows that teach a warm-up habit.
instructions: 1. Stand tall with your feet hip width apart and your weight balanced. ; 2. Brace your trunk lightly and let your arms swing naturally. ; 3. Drive one knee up toward hip height without letting your torso lean back. ; 4. Lower that foot under control and immediately raise the opposite knee. ; 5. Keep the standing leg long and the hips level as you alternate sides. ; 6. Continue for the prescribed time, then move straight onto the bike.
commonMistakes: Leaning the torso back to lift the knee higher, which shifts work into the lower back.; Rushing the tempo, so the hip never travels through a full range.; Holding static stretches here instead of moving, which misses the point of the drill.; Skipping the warm-up before hard efforts, when rapid force production matters most.
shortDescription: Standing dynamic warm-up drill performed before a ride, raising one knee at a time through a controlled full range.
longDescription:
Cycling happens in one plane through a small range, so a warm-up that only repeats the pedal stroke leaves most of the hip untouched. This clip shows the alternative: a standing dynamic drill where each knee is driven up in turn while the standing leg stays tall and stable, taking the hip through a range the bike never reaches. Warming muscle tissue raises rate of force development by roughly three and a half percent per degree, which is why a few minutes of movement before hard efforts is worth the time.

For a catalog this clip belongs in warm-up and movement-prep libraries rather than the cardio set. Use it in pre-ride sequences, class intros, and mobility screens for riders.

name: Dead Bug
tags: dead bug; core stability; anti-extension; supine; bodyweight; warm up
benefits: Trains anti-extension core control in a position that keeps load off the spine.; Needs nothing but a mat, so it fits home, travel and rehab adjacent programming.; Scales in both directions by changing limb range or adding light external load.
useCases: Warm-up and activation blocks in mobile training apps.; Beginner core onboarding flows that need a low-risk starting movement.; Low back conditioning modules in coaching and rehab adjacent platforms.; Bodyweight-only program collections and equipment-filtered library pages.
instructions: 1. Lie on your back on a mat with your arms reaching straight toward the ceiling. ; 2. Lift your feet so your hips and knees are both bent to ninety degrees. ; 3. Press your lower back gently into the floor and brace your abdominals. ; 4. Exhale and lower one arm overhead while extending the opposite leg toward the floor. ; 5. Stop just short of the floor while the lower back stays flat, then inhale and return. ; 6. Repeat with the opposite arm and leg, alternating for the prescribed reps.
commonMistakes: Letting the lower back arch off the floor, which means the core has stopped resisting extension.; Moving faster than you can breathe, which turns a control drill into a flailing exercise.; Reaching further than you can hold position, which trades range for the stability being trained.; Holding the breath throughout, which reduces the bracing the movement is meant to teach.
shortDescription: A supine anti-extension core drill that lowers one arm and the opposite leg while the lower back stays pinned down.
longDescription:
The dead bug starts lying on the back with the arms reaching up and the hips and knees bent to ninety degrees. From there one arm lowers overhead while the opposite leg extends toward the floor, and the whole job of the trunk is to stop the lower back lifting away from the ground. The rectus abdominis and transverse abdominis resist that extension, while the obliques control the diagonal loading created by using opposite limbs. Range is determined entirely by control, so reps stop the moment the back starts to arch.

As catalog inventory the dead bug is one of the highest demand core clips because it appears in warm-ups, beginner onboarding and low back programs. Its floor-level camera angle makes the lumbar contact point visible, which is the detail app users most often get wrong.

name: Dead Hang
tags: dead hang; grip strength; forearms; pull up bar; isometric; bodyweight
benefits: Builds grip and forearm endurance that carries into deadlifts, rows and pull-ups.; Lengthens the shoulders and upper back under bodyweight without any active effort.; Requires only a bar, and progress is measured in seconds rather than reps.
useCases: Timed hold sections in workout builders that count seconds, not reps.; Grip endurance work supporting deadlift and pull up progressions.; Shoulder decompression steps in recovery focused sequences.; First rung of a calisthenics pull up ladder for beginners.
instructions: 1. Set a bench or box under a secure pull-up bar so you can reach it without jumping. ; 2. Take an overhand grip slightly wider than shoulder width with the thumbs wrapped around the bar. ; 3. Step off the support and let your body hang with the arms straight. ; 4. Keep the neck long and let the shoulders relax toward the ears in a passive hang. ; 5. Squeeze the glutes lightly and hold the legs still so the body does not swing. ; 6. Hold for the prescribed time, then step back onto the support before releasing the bar.
commonMistakes: Jumping to the bar and dropping off it, which loads cold shoulders and wrists at speed.; Gripping without wrapping the thumb, which ends the hang well before the forearms are trained.; Holding the arms slightly bent, which fatigues the biceps and hides the grip work.; Letting the body swing, which spreads the load unevenly across the shoulders.
shortDescription: An isometric hang from an overhead bar that loads the grip and forearm flexors while the upper body decompresses.
longDescription:
The dead hang is a timed isometric hold rather than a rep-based exercise. Hanging from an overhead bar with straight arms puts the whole bodyweight through the hands, so the finger and wrist flexors of the forearm are the limiting tissue and the set usually ends when grip fails. Above that, the lats, scapular stabilizers and shoulders are loaded passively while the spine lengthens under gravity. Keeping the legs still and the trunk lightly braced stops the body swinging and keeps the load even across both shoulders.

For a product catalog the dead hang is a useful clip because duration-based holds are underrepresented in most libraries. It fits grip training blocks, pull-up progression ladders, mobility and decompression sequences, and any app flow that needs a timed rather than counted movement.

name: Decline Barbell Bench Press

benefits: Shortens the pressing range compared with a flat bench, which some lifters tolerate better at the shoulder.; Keeps triceps involvement high, so it doubles as elbow extension volume on a chest day.; Completes the bench-angle set, giving a third loading position for the pectorals.
useCases: Chest day templates in a strength training app; Barbell equipment filters in a browsable exercise library; Bench-angle comparison content for coaches and program builders; Progression paths that move from flat to incline and decline pressing
instructions: 1. Set a decline bench, load the bar, and hook your feet securely under the leg pad. ; 2. Lie back with your eyes under the bar and grip it just outside shoulder width. ; 3. Pinch your shoulder blades together and drive them into the pad, then take the lift-off with a spotter. ; 4. The decline barbell bench press puts the torso head-down with the feet hooked under a pad, which lowers the pressing angle and shortens the bar path. The pectoralis major is the prime mover, the triceps extend the elbows, and the front deltoid contributes less than on an incline. EMG comparison of flat, inclined and declined benching found similar pectoral activity in all three positions.

Setup carries most of the risk. Shoulder blades stay pinned to the pad, a spotter helps with the lift-off, and the bar descends under control to the sternum rather than bouncing.

As an asset the decline press completes a barbell chest set alongside flat and incline pressing, so it earns a place in barbell equipment filters, chest day templates and bench-angle progressions.

The decline crunch is a crunch performed head-down on an angled bench with the feet secured.
