A neutral grip pull-up uses a V-bar or parallel handles so the palms face each other and the forearms stay mid-position. Compared with a pronated pull-up the shoulder is not driven into abduction and internal rotation, a common source of impingement complaints, and the elbows track closer to the ribs. The lats and rhomboids remain the prime movers, with the biceps, brachialis, mid trapezius and rear delts assisting more than in a wide pronated pull-up.

For a catalog this is the shoulder-friendly member of the pull-up family and a frequent request in programs for older or rehab-adjacent users. Use it in bodyweight equipment filters, calisthenics and hybrid training templates, and grip comparison content showing pronated, supinated and neutral pull-ups from one mannequin.

name: Nordic Hamstring Curl
tags: nordic hamstring curl; hamstrings; eccentric; bodyweight; posterior chain; injury prevention
benefits: Loads the hamstrings eccentrically at the long lengths where strains occur.; Needs only an ankle anchor, so it travels to any field, gym or garage.; Progresses by range and tempo rather than by adding external load.
useCases: Injury-prevention blocks in team-sport training apps.; Preseason hamstring programs for running and field sports.; Rehab-adjacent education content on eccentric training.; The advanced hamstring slot in a bodyweight program builder.
instructions: 1. Kneel on a pad with your knees bent and the tops of your feet flat on the floor. ; 2. Anchor your ankles under a loaded barbell, a fixed pad, or a partner's hands. ; 3. Stand tall through the hips so knees, hips and shoulders form one line. ; 4. Reach your arms forward and lower your torso slowly, keeping the hips extended. ; 5. Catch yourself on your hands once you can no longer control the descent. ; 6. Push back just enough to let the hamstrings pull you upright, then repeat.
commonMistakes: Breaking at the hips so the movement becomes a bow, which unloads the hamstrings.; Dropping fast once it gets hard, which removes the eccentric stimulus the exercise exists for.; Pushing hard off the floor every rep, so the arms do the work the hamstrings should.; Starting at full range with no assistance, which usually ends in a cramp or a strain.
shortDescription: A kneeling bodyweight curl where the hamstrings resist the whole body lowering toward the floor under eccentric control.
longDescription:
The Nordic hamstring curl is a kneeling eccentric exercise. Your ankles are pinned, usually under a loaded barbell or a partner's hands, and you lower your torso toward the floor while holding the hips extended so the knee flexors alone control the descent. Most people run out of control partway down, catch themselves on their hands, then push back just enough to let the hamstrings finish the rep. Peak knee flexor force here is high, which is why it is studied so heavily as a hamstring strain intervention.

In a catalog this is the flagship hamstring clip for field-sport and rehab audiences. It supports injury-prevention programs, preseason blocks, warm-up templates for running clubs, and content explaining eccentric training, where a loop of the slow descent says far more than a still photo.

name: Pallof Press
tags: pallof press; anti-rotation; core; obliques; cable machine; band
benefits: Trains the trunk to resist rotation rather than produce it.; Isometric bracing loads the obliques and deep abdominals without spinal flexion.; Scales cleanly by stepping closer to or further from the anchor.
useCases: Core block in strength and athletic program templates.; Anti-rotation entry that resolves for both cable and band filters.; Teaching content on resisting rotation alongside planks and carries.; Bracing warm-up before heavy squatting or pressing.
instructions: 1. Set a cable pulley or anchor a band at chest height. ; 2. Stand side-on to the anchor and take the handle in both hands with your fingers laced. ; 3. Step away until the cable is under tension and set your feet slightly wider than shoulder width. ; 4. Pull the handle in to the center of your chest and brace your abs hard. ; 5. Press the handle straight out and hold for two to three seconds without letting your torso turn. ; 6. Return the handle to your chest under control, finish the set, then turn around and face the other way.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips and shoulders rotate toward the anchor, which removes the anti-rotation demand entirely.; Standing too close to the stack, so there is no tension left to resist at full extension.; Holding your breath through the press, which usually means the load is beyond what your bracing can hold.; Pressing off-center or across the body, which turns the drill into an unsteady one-arm chest press.
shortDescription: A standing anti-rotation drill: hold a cable or band at chest height side-on and press it out without letting the torso turn.
longDescription:
Despite the name, the Pallof press is a core exercise rather than a pressing exercise. You stand side-on to a cable stack or an anchored band set at chest height, hold the handle against your chest with both hands, then press it out and back while the tension tries to rotate you toward the anchor. The abs are the target and the demand is isometric, so the job is to stop the hips turning as the arms extend. The obliques and transverse abdominis are the muscles resisting that rotation.

For a library this is the clearest way to show anti-rotation, a category most catalogs cover only with planks. It belongs in core blocks, in both cable and band equipment filters, and in coaching content on resisting movement rather than producing it.

name: Parallel Bar Dips
tags: parallel bar dips; chest exercise; triceps; bodyweight; push day; calisthenics
benefits: Builds serious chest, triceps, and front-shoulder strength with bodyweight only.; Trains a vertical press pattern that complements overhead and bench work.; Develops the body-control needed for advanced calisthenics.
useCases: Calisthenics and bodyweight strength programming in fitness apps; Park and minimal-equipment workout content; Push-day inventory for home-and-travel program tracks; Hero clips and thumbnails for bodyweight strength content
instructions: 1. Grip the parallel bars with palms facing each other and press up to a strong, locked-out start position. ; 2. Brace your core, squeeze the glutes, and cross the ankles to keep the body in a tight line. ; 3. Lean your torso slightly forward to bias the chest, or stay upright to bias the triceps. ; 4. Lower yourself slowly over 2 to 3 seconds until your shoulders drop just below your elbows. ; 5. Pause briefly at the bottom with the chest open and the body still controlled. ; 6. Press back up to full lockout by driving through the chest and triceps in one smooth motion.
commonMistakes: Letting the shoulders shrug up to the ears at the bottom, which strains the front shoulders.; Cutting the depth short and only doing the easy top half of the rep.; Swinging the legs to use momentum, which removes the controlled loading the dip is meant to deliver.; Flaring the elbows wide on the press, which puts unnecessary strain on the joint.
shortDescription: A bodyweight dip on parallel bars that builds the chest and triceps — one of the most demanding pure-bodyweight upper-body lifts.
longDescription:
Parallel bar dips are one of the most respected bodyweight upper-body exercises in any program. Suspended between two bars, the lifter lowers themselves until the shoulders dip below the elbows, then drives back up to lockout. The movement loads the chest, triceps, and front shoulders hard and exposes any weakness in upper-body strength.

For app and content use, this clip is a hero piece for calisthenics programs, bodyweight strength tracks, and gymnastics-adjacent content. It also pairs naturally with pull-up and push-up content as part of a complete bodyweight push-pull library for home, park, or minimal-equipment programming.

name: Pause Squat
tags: pause squat; bodyweight; quadriceps; squat; tempo; isometric
benefits: Removes the stretch reflex, so the legs produce every bit of the force.; Builds control and bracing at depth before external load is added.; Needs no equipment, so it scales any bodyweight lower body plan.
useCases: Tempo and time under tension blocks in a bodyweight plan.; Squat technique content teaching control at depth.; Progression step before external load is added to the squat.; Isometric hold demo for apps that display a pause count.
instructions: 1. Stand with your feet slightly wider than hip width and toes turned out a little. ; 2. Pull your shoulders down and back and brace your trunk. ; 3. Push the hips back and bend the knees together to descend. ; 4. Lower until your thighs are at least parallel, keeping the heels down. ; 5. Hold the bottom position for about a second without relaxing. ; 6. Press through the whole foot to stand and reset before the next rep.
commonMistakes: Relaxing in the bottom position, which lets the chest fold forward on the way up.; Bouncing out of the pause, which is the exact reflex the hold is meant to remove.; Letting the heels lift, which shifts load onto the front of the knees.; Holding far longer than a second, which fatigues the position instead of training it.
shortDescription: A bodyweight squat held still at the bottom, removing the bounce so the legs restart from a dead stop.
longDescription:
The pause squat is an ordinary squat with a deliberate stop at the bottom. You descend under control until the thighs are at least parallel, hold with the trunk braced, then stand. The pause removes the stretch reflex, so nothing helps you out of the hole and the quadriceps and glutes have to start the rep cold. The hold stays short, around a one-thousand-one count, and staying tight in the bottom position is what makes it work: lose the brace and the chest folds forward as you try to stand.

As an asset the pause is hard to convey in a photograph and obvious in a loop, which is why this clip is worth carrying. It suits bodyweight equipment filters, tempo and time under tension programming, and technique content teaching control at depth before load is added.

name: Pendlay Row
tags: pendlay row; barbell row; dead stop; back; upper back; horizontal pull
benefits: Every rep starts from a dead stop, so no momentum carries over.; Trains explosive pulling strength for the lats and mid back.; Reinforces the hinge position under repeated heavy loading.
useCases: Barbell filter entry for the dead stop row in a pull day.; Power focused rowing in powerlifting and athletic accessory blocks.; Coaching content contrasting dead stop and continuous rows.; Clean loop point for interval and rep-count clip displays.
instructions: 1. Set a loaded barbell on the floor directly in front of your shins. ; 2. Bend forward at the hips until your back is almost level above the bar. ; 3. Take a double overhand grip just outside your knees. ; 4. Brace your abdominals and set your shoulder blades before pulling. ; 5. Pull the bar explosively to your belly button, driving your elbows back. ; 6. Return the bar to the floor, let it settle, then start the next rep.
commonMistakes: Bouncing the bar off the floor, which removes the dead stop the exercise is built around.; Raising the torso as the bar comes up, so the hips finish the lift instead of the back.; Rounding the lower back on the reset, which loads the lumbar spine at the worst moment.; Pulling slowly, which turns a power exercise into an ordinary heavy row.
shortDescription: A barbell row reset on the floor each rep, pulled explosively from a dead stop to the abdomen.
longDescription:
The Pendlay row differs from a standard bent over row in one way that changes everything: the bar returns to the floor and comes to a complete dead stop between reps. You hinge until the torso is close to parallel, take a double overhand grip with the bar over your shins, then pull explosively to the belly button while retracting the shoulder blades. Every rep therefore starts from zero momentum, which is why it is programmed for pulling power rather than time under tension. The lats and mid back drive the pull while the erectors, biceps and rear delts support it.

For a library this is the strength-and-power row, distinct from the hypertrophy rows around it. It fits barbell equipment filters, powerlifting and athletic accessory blocks, and coaching content that contrasts dead stop with continuous rowing.

name: Pendulum Squat / V-Squat
tags: pendulum squat; v squat; machine; quadriceps; squat; gym machine
benefits: The arc keeps tension high in the stretched position where quad growth is driven.; Back support removes spinal loading from a deep squat pattern.; The guided path lets you train close to failure without a spotter.
useCases: Arc-path squat entry in a machine equipment filter.; Quad-focused hypertrophy block in leg day templates.; Comparison content against the hack squat and leg press.; Equipment orientation content for clubs adding a pendulum machine.
instructions: 1. Load the machine and set the foot plate to suit your height and ankle range. ; 2. Position your back and shoulders against the pads with your hips settled. ; 3. Place your feet hip to shoulder width on the plate, toes turned out slightly. ; 4. Release the safeties and brace your trunk. ; 5. Descend along the arc until your thighs pass parallel. ; 6. Drive through the feet to return, stopping just short of knee lockout.
commonMistakes: Letting the head and hips fall out of line, which twists the load off the arc.; Riding the machine down quickly, which wastes the loaded stretch at the bottom.; Letting the heels lift off the plate, which shifts the load onto the knees.; Skipping the warm-up before loading a deep, stretched squat position.
shortDescription: A machine squat on a counterbalanced arc, keeping the torso supported while the quads work through deep range.
longDescription:
The pendulum squat runs the body along a swinging arc rather than a straight rail. Your back and shoulders sit against a pad that travels with you and your feet stay planted on an adjustable plate, so the machine holds position while you squat deep. A counterbalance keeps the motion smooth, and the arc gives a resistance curve that stays heavy in the stretched bottom position instead of falling away. The quadriceps are the prime movers, with the glutes taking over through the transition out of the bottom and the hamstrings stabilizing.

For a catalog this is a high demand machine that almost no animation library carries. It suits machine equipment filters, quad-focused hypertrophy blocks, and comparison content set against the hack squat and leg press.

name: Plate Forward Lunge
tags: plate forward lunge; lunge; quad exercise; glutes; single leg; leg day
benefits: Builds quad and glute strength with a single-leg pattern that fixes side imbalances.; Trains the core to brace under a front-loaded position.; Easy to scale up by simply choosing a heavier plate.
useCases: Beginner-to-intermediate leg-day programming in fitness apps; Athletic-prep single-leg blocks in performance tracks; Gym-floor minimal-equipment program content; Single-leg strength education in coaching platforms
instructions: 1. Stand tall holding a weight plate horizontally against your upper chest with both hands. ; 2. Brace your core, pull your shoulders back, and set your feet hip-width apart. ; 3. Step one foot forward into a long stride, lowering your back knee toward the floor. ; 4. Stop when your front thigh is roughly parallel to the floor and your back knee hovers above it. ; 5. Drive through the heel of your front foot to push back to the standing start position. ; 6. Repeat on the opposite leg, alternating sides for the full set with the plate locked at the chest.
commonMistakes: Letting the front knee cave inward on the step, which strains the joint and reduces force production.; Taking a stride that's too short, which puts the front knee far past the toes and overloads it.; Leaning the torso forward over the plate instead of staying upright through the descent.; Pushing off the back foot to stand up, which steals work from the front leg the lunge is meant to load.
shortDescription: A forward lunge holding a weight plate at the chest that loads the quads and glutes through a single-leg step — the gym-floor classic.
longDescription:
The plate forward lunge takes the bodyweight lunge and adds load by holding a weight plate against the chest. The forward step loads the quads and glutes of the working leg, while holding the plate at the chest forces the core to brace and the torso to stay tall. It's a clean way to introduce loaded single-leg work without needing dumbbells or a barbell.

For app and content use, this clip is a strong fit for beginner-to-intermediate strength programs, athletic prep tracks, and gym-floor content where users only need a plate. It pairs naturally with goblet squat and step-up content as part of a complete single-leg leg-day library.

name: Plate Front Raise
tags: plate front raise; weight plate; shoulders; front raise; deltoids; isolation
benefits: One plate is all the equipment needed, which suits crowded or minimally kitted gyms.; The neutral two-handed grip keeps the wrists in a comfortable position.; Strict single-joint work makes front deltoid volume easy to count in a program.
useCases: Minimal-equipment shoulder blocks in gym app programs.; Library entries for lifters who can find a plate but not a matched pair.; Beginner front raise progression before dumbbell versions.; Comparison content against dumbbell and cable front raises.
instructions: 1. Pick up a weight plate and hold it at the three and nine o'clock positions with your palms facing each other. ; 2. Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart and your shoulders pulled back. ; 3. Let the plate hang a few inches in front of your thighs without touching them. ; 4. Brace your abs and keep a slight bend in your elbows. ; 5. Raise the plate in front of you until it is just above parallel with the floor, then pause. ; 6. Lower it slowly back to the start without letting it rest against your body.
commonMistakes: Swinging the plate up with a hip drive, which removes the front of the deltoid from the lift.; Letting the plate touch the thighs between reps, which unloads the shoulder at the bottom.; Gripping too low on the plate, so it tips away from the wrists and the set ends on grip.; Programming it only alongside heavy pressing, which piles more volume on an already busy anterior deltoid.
shortDescription: A front raise holding one weight plate at the three and nine o'clock positions and lifting it to shoulder height.
longDescription:
The plate front raise swaps two dumbbells for a single weight plate gripped at the three and nine o'clock positions with the palms facing each other. You stand tall, keep the plate a few inches clear of your thighs, and raise it in front of you to just above parallel with the floor before lowering it slowly. It is a shoulder isolation movement, simple enough for beginners, but it demands strict technique because momentum is the easy way out. The path is plain shoulder flexion with the abs braced throughout.

In a catalog this is the front raise that needs one piece of kit and no matched pair, which makes it useful in busy-gym and minimal-equipment programming. It also shows a plate-holding grip no other shoulder animation in the library carries.

name: Plate Pinch
tags: plate pinch; grip strength; forearms; isometric; static hold; accessory
benefits: Trains thumb-to-finger pinch strength that crushing-grip work does not reach.; Simple to load and progress by adding plates or thinner plate stacks.; Requires almost no space or setup, so it fits at the end of any session.
useCases: Grip strength accessory block in a strength program builder.; Strongman and armwrestling content library entry.; Forearm focused finisher slot at the end of a session.; Timed exercise widget demo where the set ends when grip fails.
instructions: 1. Stand one or two plates on end with the smooth sides facing out. ; 2. Set your thumb on one face and your flat fingers on the other, avoiding any hook around the rim. ; 3. Squeeze the plates together and stand up tall with the arm hanging at your side. ; 4. Keep your shoulder packed and your wrist neutral, with no swinging. ; 5. Hold until the grip is about to fail, aiming for twenty to thirty seconds. ; 6. Set the plates down under control and repeat with the other hand.
commonMistakes: Hooking the fingers around the plate rim, which turns a pinch into a hold and removes the thumb demand.; Letting the wrist bend under load, which cuts pinch force before the fingers actually fatigue.; Swinging the arm to reduce the felt load, which shortens the useful time under tension.; Programming it before heavy pulling work, which leaves grip fatigued for the main lifts.
shortDescription: Static grip hold in which you pinch a pair of weight plates between the thumb and flat fingers for time.
longDescription:
The plate pinch trains pinch grip, which is thumb-against-fingers strength rather than the crushing grip a barbell trains. You hold one or two plates smooth side out between the pad of the thumb and the flat of the fingers, stand tall and hold until the grip fails. It is a static isolation movement for the forearms, and stacking several thin plates is harder to hold than one heavy plate of the same weight. The clinical literature on pulp-to-pulp pinch strength shows how sensitive the measurement is to finger position, which is why a hooked finger makes the exercise easier and defeats the point.

For a catalog this fills a gap most exercise libraries skip. Grip programs, strongman content and climbing-adjacent apps all need a pinch-hold clip.

name: Power Clean - no overhead press
tags: power clean; barbell; olympic lift; triple extension; explosive; full body
benefits: Trains triple extension of the hips, knees and ankles against a heavy external load.; The whole-body timing demand makes it a coordination lift as much as a strength lift.; It ends at the shoulders rather than overhead, so the shoulder demand stays low.
useCases: Power block in athletic performance program templates.; Barbell filter entry for libraries that carry Olympic lift derivatives.; Phase-by-phase coaching content on the pull, the extension and the catch.; Advanced difficulty filter for programs aimed at trained lifters.
instructions: 1. Set a loaded barbell on the floor about an inch in front of your shins with your feet hip-width apart. ; 2. Squat down and grip the bar just outside your knees with your hips below your shoulders and your chest up. ; 3. Extend your hips and knees to lift the bar while keeping your torso angle and the bar close to your legs. ; 4. As the bar passes your knees, drive your hips forward and explosively extend hips, knees and ankles. ; 5. Shrug and pull your elbows high, then whip them under the bar to catch it on your front deltoids in a quarter squat. ; 6. Stand tall to finish the rep, then lower the bar back to the floor under control.
commonMistakes: Pulling with the arms early, which spends the leg drive that should be moving the bar.; Letting the bar drift away from the body, which throws the catch forward and out of position.; Catching with the elbows low, so the bar rolls onto the wrists instead of resting on the shoulders.; Loading it before the sequence is grooved, which turns an explosive lift into a slow bent-over row.
shortDescription: An explosive barbell pull from the floor to a front rack catch on the shoulders, finishing without any overhead press.
longDescription:
The power clean moves a barbell from the floor to the shoulders in one explosive sequence. It breaks into a first pull that lifts the bar while the torso angle holds, a transition as the bar passes the knees, a second pull that extends hips, knees and ankles before a high shrug, and a catch where the elbows whip under the bar and receive it on the front deltoids. The lower body and hips generate most of the force, and the full sequence can take years to master. Muscle activity starts in the back and the posterior lower limb, then the arms, then the trunk and quadriceps.

For a catalog this is the power entry athletic programs need and most animation libraries lack. It suits barbell filters, advanced difficulty filters, and phase-by-phase coaching content.

name: Pull Ups
tags: pull ups; lats; back exercise; bodyweight; vertical pull; calisthenics
benefits: Builds the lats, biceps, and upper back with one of the highest-yield bodyweight lifts.; Develops the relative strength needed for advanced calisthenics and athletic work.; Reinforces shoulder health by training the back muscles that stabilize the joint.
useCases: Pull-day programming in any strength training app; Calisthenics and bodyweight strength tracks; Pull-up progression modules in coaching platforms; Hero clips and thumbnails for back and pulling content
instructions: 1. Reach up and grip a fixed pull-up bar with palms facing forward, hands slightly wider than shoulders. ; 2. Hang from the bar with arms fully extended, then engage the lats by pulling the shoulder blades down. ; 3. Brace your core, squeeze the glutes, and cross the ankles to keep the body in a tight line. ; 4. Pull yourself up by driving the elbows down toward the ribs until your chin clears the bar. ; 5. Pause briefly at the top with the chin over the bar, squeezing the lats and upper back. ; 6. Lower yourself slowly over 2 to 3 seconds back to a full dead hang before the next rep.
commonMistakes: Kipping the legs to swing up instead of pulling cleanly with the back and arms.; Cutting the bottom range short and never reaching a full dead hang, which trains a fraction of the lift.; Leading with the chin instead of the chest, which puts strain on the neck.; Dropping fast at the top and skipping the slow descent, where most pull-up strength is built.
shortDescription: The classic bodyweight vertical pull that builds the lats, biceps, and upper back — the benchmark for upper-body pulling strength.
longDescription:
The pull-up is the benchmark bodyweight upper-body exercise. Hanging from a fixed bar with palms facing forward, the lifter pulls the body up until the chin clears the bar, then lowers under control. It builds the lats, biceps, and the upper back, and it's one of the clearest measures of relative pulling strength.

For app and content use, this clip is essential inventory for any strength library, calisthenics program, and pull-day track. It also anchors any pull-up progression module and serves as a recognizable hero piece for content aimed at lifters chasing their first strict rep.

name: Push Jerk
tags: push jerk; olympic lifting; barbell; overhead; explosive; shoulders
benefits: Moves heavier overhead loads than a strict press by adding leg drive.; Trains the dip and drive timing that transfers to the split jerk.; Builds overhead lockout strength and stability under speed.
useCases: Overhead lift entry in a CrossFit or weightlifting exercise library; Overhead power block in a strength and conditioning program builder; Technique explainer contrasting push jerk, power jerk and split jerk; Warm-up or primer clip before jerk-focused training sessions
instructions: 1. Take the bar in a front rack across the shoulders with the elbows down and in front of the bar. ; 2. Set your feet in your squat stance with your weight balanced over the whole foot. ; 3. Brace your trunk and dip by bending the knees only, keeping the torso vertical. ; 4. Reverse hard and drive the bar off the shoulders with the legs. ; 5. Punch the elbows into lockout overhead and receive the bar in a partial squat with the feet planted. ; 6. Stand up with the bar stable overhead, then lower it back to the rack position.
commonMistakes: Dipping too deep, which slows the reversal and turns the lift into a slow press.; Letting the torso pitch forward in the dip, which sends the bar out in front of the body.; Pressing with the arms before the legs finish, which loses the drive and stalls the bar at eye level.; Receiving with soft elbows, which puts the load on the shoulder joint instead of the skeleton.
shortDescription: Barbell overhead lift driven by a short leg dip, received in a partial squat with the feet planted.
longDescription:
The push jerk moves a barbell from the front rack to overhead using the legs, not the arms. You dip about ten percent of your height with a vertical torso, drive the bar up off the shoulders, then punch the elbows into lockout and settle into a partial squat before standing. What separates it from the power jerk is the feet: in a push jerk they stay connected to the floor in the squat stance instead of moving. The quadriceps are the target, with the shoulders, traps and triceps supporting.

In a product library this clip covers the overhead lift that CrossFit and weightlifting programs use most often, and the dip-drive-lockout sequence is exactly the kind of timing detail a static image cannot carry.

name: Push Up
tags: push up; chest exercise; bodyweight; push day; horizontal press; home workout
benefits: Builds the chest, triceps, and front shoulders without any equipment.; Reinforces a strong full-body plank shape under pressing load.; Scales infinitely from incline beginner versions to advanced weighted variations.
useCases: Beginner onboarding programming in fitness apps; Home-and-travel push-day workouts with no equipment; Warm-up flows for upper-body strength sessions; Push pattern education in coaching platforms
instructions: 1. Set up in a high-plank position with your hands slightly wider than shoulder width and arms locked. ; 2. Brace your core, squeeze the glutes, and keep your body in a straight line from head to heels. ; 3. Lower your chest slowly toward the floor over 2 to 3 seconds, keeping the elbows at about 45 degrees. ; 4. Stop when your chest hovers just above the floor, holding the bottom briefly with full body tension. ; 5. Press back up by driving the floor away through the palms until the arms reach full extension. ; 6. Reset your breath and repeat for the full set, keeping the body line tight on every rep.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips sag toward the floor, which removes the core demand and strains the lower back.; Letting the elbows flare to 90 degrees, which strains the front shoulders and reduces chest engagement.; Cutting the depth short and only pressing the top half of the rep instead of touching the chest down.; Letting the head poke forward instead of keeping the neck in line with the spine.
shortDescription: The most foundational bodyweight push lift — trains the chest, triceps, and front shoulders with a single, scalable pattern.
longDescription:
The push-up is the most foundational bodyweight upper-body exercise. From a high-plank position, the lifter lowers the chest to the floor and presses back up, loading the chest, triceps, and front shoulders through a controlled horizontal press. It scales endlessly: incline for beginners, decline or weighted for advanced lifters.

For app and content use, this clip is non-negotiable inventory for any beginner program, home-and-travel track, or warm-up flow. It also serves as the anchor of any push pattern progression in coaching platforms and as a clean teaching piece for movement-quality content aimed at brand-new lifters.

name: Reverse-Grip Barbell Bench Press
tags: chest; barbell; bench press; reverse grip; upper chest; push
benefits: Increases upper chest and biceps involvement compared with a pronated grip on the same flat bench.; Gives a fresh pressing stimulus for lifters with no access to an adjustable incline bench.; Alters the wrist and shoulder position, which some lifters find kinder on a sore shoulder.
useCases: Grip-variation blocks in barbell strength programming; Barbell equipment filters in an exercise library; Upper-chest options for flat-bench-only gym setups; Coaching content comparing grip positions on the bench press
instructions: 1. Set the rack height on a flat bench and load the bar conservatively for your first sets. ; 2. Lie back with your feet planted and take the bar with an underhand grip a little wider than shoulder width. ; 3. Set your shoulder blades into the bench, then unrack the bar with a spotter's help. ; 4. Lower the bar slowly to your mid-chest, keeping your wrists stacked over your forearms. ; 5. Pause without letting the bar rest on your chest, then press it back up. ; 6. Stop short of locking the elbows and keep your glutes and shoulder blades on the bench throughout.
commonMistakes: Unracking a supinated bar without a spotter risks losing it backward before the first rep is under control.; Letting the wrists bend back under load puts the bar behind the forearm and strains the wrist joint.; Loading it like a standard bench press overwhelms an unfamiliar grip and forces the form to break down.; Lifting the feet or hips off the bench to grind a rep removes the stable base the press depends on.
shortDescription: Flat barbell press taken with an underhand grip, which shifts pressing emphasis toward the upper chest.
longDescription:
The reverse-grip barbell bench press keeps the flat bench setup but supinates the hands so the palms face the head. That rotation changes which fibers work: bench press EMG shows a supinated grip increases activity in the clavicular portion of the pectoralis major and in the biceps brachii compared with a pronated grip. The triceps still extend the elbows.

The grip is the risk. Unracking and re-racking a supinated bar is awkward and the wrists sit in a less familiar position, so a spotter and conservative loading are sensible.

As an asset it is the upper-chest alternative for lifters restricted to a flat bench, useful in barbell filters, grip-variation content and builders that rotate pressing stimulus without changing bench angle.

name: Reverse Grip Barbell Curl
tags: reverse grip barbell curl; reverse curl; forearms; barbell; grip strength; arms
benefits: Puts the forearm elbow flexors in their strongest pulling position.; Builds the grip and wrist strength that carries into rows and deadlifts.; Adds forearm thickness that palms-up curls alone tend to miss.
useCases: Forearm and grip accessory blocks in a strength app.; Pronated curl option in barbell-based arm libraries.; Technique content contrasting supinated and pronated curls.; Arm day templates that need a non-biceps elbow flexion option.
instructions: 1. Load a barbell and stand upright with your feet about hip-width apart. ; 2. Grip the bar palms down with your hands roughly shoulder-width apart. ; 3. Let the bar rest at your thighs with your elbows straight and pinned to your sides. ; 4. Curl the bar up by bending only at the elbows, keeping your wrists straight. ; 5. Stop when the bar reaches chest height and hold the top briefly. ; 6. Lower the bar under control to full extension and repeat.
commonMistakes: Loading it like a standard curl, which collapses the wrists long before the forearms are trained.; Letting the wrists bend back under the bar, which moves the strain to the wrist joint.; Swinging the elbows forward, which turns the lift into a front raise.; Rocking the torso to start each rep, so momentum replaces the elbow flexors.
shortDescription: A standing barbell curl taken with the palms facing down, shifting the work from the biceps onto the forearms.
longDescription:
The reverse grip barbell curl is a standard curl performed with a pronated grip. Palms face the floor, hands sit about shoulder width, and the elbows stay pinned to the ribs while only the forearms move. Turning the hands over takes the biceps out of its strongest line of pull and hands the job to the forearm elbow flexors, which is why the forearms are the target here and the biceps only support. Expect the working weight to fall sharply against a normal curl, because grip and wrist position, not elbow strength, set the ceiling here.

For a library this clip fills the forearm and grip gap most catalogs leave empty. It suits arm accessory blocks, grip work for climbers and lifters, barbell equipment filters, and technique content that contrasts supinated and pronated curling side by side.

name: Reverse-Grip Tricep Pushdown

longDescription:
The reverse-grip tricep pushdown is a straight-bar pushdown performed with a supinated grip. You stand facing a high pulley, take the bar palms up, tuck your elbows against your ribs and press down until the arms are almost straight. Turning the hands over cuts how much the forearms contribute and keeps the elbow tight to the side, which lets the arm travel further behind the body and load the long head of the triceps harder. Elbow position decides it: let them drift forward and the lats take over.

MoveKit collapses long-head bias into a single Triceps group, so that emphasis lives in the copy. For a library the clip covers a grip variation buyers ask for by name and fits arm accessory blocks, cable machine filters, and elbow-friendly programming for lifters who avoid overhead work.

name: Reverse Hack Squat
tags: reverse hack squat; hack squat machine; machine; glutes; hamstrings; posterior chain
benefits: Loads the glutes and hamstrings on a machine most gyms already own.; The chest pad supports the trunk, so the lower back is not the limiting factor.; Gives a second, posterior chain exercise from a single piece of equipment.
useCases: Hack squat machine entry filed under the machine equipment filter.; Posterior chain accessory slot in lower body templates.; Paired content showing both directions on the hack squat machine.; Alternative hamstring asset when no leg curl station is available.
instructions: 1. Load the machine and step onto the platform facing the pad. ; 2. Rest your chest on the pad with your shoulders under the shoulder pads. ; 3. Set your feet at shoulder width, slightly higher on the platform. ; 4. Extend the legs, release the safeties and take the load. ; 5. Push the hips back and lower until the knees reach about 90 degrees. ; 6. Drive through the heels to return without locking the knees.
commonMistakes: Keeping the torso vertical, which turns it back into a quad-dominant hack squat.; Letting the knees track well past the toes, which loads the joint and drops hip involvement.; Locking out at the top, which unloads the glutes and hamstrings between reps.; Dropping into the bottom, which loads the hamstrings faster than they can control.
shortDescription: A hack squat performed facing the machine, shifting the squat pattern onto the glutes and hamstrings.
longDescription:
The reverse hack squat turns you around on the hack squat machine so your chest rests against the carriage pad instead of your back. From there the torso can lean forward and the hips travel through more flexion, which moves the squat pattern onto the posterior chain. The hamstrings become the target with the glutes, quadriceps and calves assisting, which turns an anterior loaded machine into a posterior chain tool. The quadriceps still work, but they are no longer the point.

This clip fills a gap most catalogs miss, because the machine looks identical to a hack squat and the difference is entirely body orientation. It suits machine equipment filters, posterior chain accessory blocks, and paired content on one machine.

name: Reverse Hyperextension
tags: reverse hyperextension; glutes; hip extension; posterior chain; bodyweight; bench
benefits: Trains hip extension with the torso supported, so the lower back is not the limiter.; Needs only a bench, so it works in home and minimal-equipment settings.; Builds the glute and hamstring strength that carries into hinges and squats.

Reach under the bench and grip the frame so your torso cannot slide forward. ; 4. Squeeze your glutes and lift your legs behind you until your body is level. ; 5. Pause at the top without arching your lower back past flat. ; 6. Lower your legs slowly back to the hang and repeat for the prescribed reps.

shortDescription: A prone hip extension off the end of a bench, lifting the legs behind the body to drive the glutes and hamstrings.
longDescription:
The reverse hyperextension is hip extension performed from a fixed torso. You lie face down on a bench with your hips at the edge and your legs hanging free, grip the frame underneath, then lift your legs behind you until the body is level and lower them under control. The glutes drive it, the hamstrings assist and the spinal erectors hold the trunk flat. Despite the name it is not a spinal exercise: the joint that moves is the hip. Reviewed coverage of the machine version credits it with posterior chain loading and less lumbar stress than a back extension.

For a catalog this is the low-equipment posterior chain option. It fits glute-focused program blocks, back-friendly accessory work, bodyweight filters in a home-training app, and content explaining hip extension versus spinal extension.

useCases: Rear-delt accessory slots in pull and upper-body app workouts; High rep rear delt sets that stay stable once the weight gets light; Posture and shoulder-balance content for desk-bound users; Warm-up sequences before heavy pressing in program builders

Sit facing the machine with your chest against the pad and your feet flat on the floor. ; 3. Take a handle in each hand with a pronated or neutral grip and hold a fixed bend in the elbows. ; 4. Sweep both arms out and back until they reach roughly shoulder height in line with your torso. ; 5. Hold the end position for a beat without shrugging or pushing your head forward. ; 6. Return the handles slowly to the start under control, then repeat.
commonMistakes: Driving the movement by squeezing the shoulder blades turns a rear-delt fly into a rowing pattern.; Letting the head jut forward as the arms open loads the neck and signals a load that is too heavy.; Bending and straightening the elbows through the rep converts the fly into a partial row.; Pulling the chest off the pad to gain range restores the trunk demand the machine was chosen to remove.
shortDescription: Chest-supported machine fly performed in reverse, opening the arms backward to load the rear deltoids.
longDescription:
The reverse pec deck reverses the pec deck to train the back of the shoulder. You sit facing the pad with the handles at torso height and sweep the arms outward and back with the elbow angle fixed. The posterior deltoid does the horizontal shoulder abduction, with the trapezius and mid-back muscles assisting near end range.

The chest pad is what makes it useful. It removes the trunk stability demand of a bent-over reverse fly, and the cue is to move at the shoulder socket rather than squeeze the shoulder blades together.

In a catalog this clip serves the rear-delt and posture segment: shoulder accessory slots, machine equipment filters and upper-body balance content that must show arm movement rather than scapular retraction.

name: Romanian Deadlift Hamstring Sweeps
tags: hamstring sweeps; romanian deadlift; bodyweight; hamstrings; dynamic stretch; warm up
benefits: Moves the hamstrings through range under active control instead of a static hold.; Rehearses the hip hinge pattern before loaded deadlift or RDL work.; Needs no equipment and only a few meters of floor space.
useCases: Bodyweight equipment filter in a mobility or running app.; Dynamic warm-up sequence before running or lifting.; Hip hinge teaching asset ahead of loaded RDL content.; Cooldown and mobility library for coaching platforms.
instructions: 1. Stand tall with your feet under your hips and your arms by your sides. ; 2. Step one foot forward and set the heel down with the toes lifted. ; 3. Keep both legs close to straight and brace your trunk lightly. ; 4. Hinge at the hips and sweep both arms down toward the front foot. ; 5. Sweep the arms back up as you drive the hips forward to stand. ; 6. Step through onto the other foot and repeat, alternating sides.
commonMistakes: Rounding the back to reach lower, which stretches the spine rather than the hamstrings.; Bending the front knee, which takes the hamstring out of the stretch entirely.; Bouncing at the bottom, which provokes a guarding response instead of range.; Treating it as a strength set, which fatigues the hamstrings before the real work.
shortDescription: A standing bodyweight hinge with an arm sweep, taking the hamstrings through range as a dynamic warm-up.
longDescription:
Hamstring sweeps take the Romanian deadlift shape and turn it into a moving warm-up. You step one foot forward with the heel down and the toes lifted, keep the legs close to straight, hinge at the hips and sweep the arms down past the front foot and back up as you stand. The same drill is used as a walking dynamic hamstring stretch and needs no equipment at all. Because it is a hinge, the hamstrings and glutes control the descent while the trunk holds a long spine exactly as in a loaded RDL, but the load is bodyweight and the goal is range rather than strength.

For a product library this covers the warm-up slot strength catalogs usually leave empty. It fits bodyweight equipment filters, pre-run and pre-lift mobility sequences, and hinge technique content.

name: Rowing Intervals
tags: rowing intervals; erg; indoor rowing; cardio; hiit; conditioning
benefits: Trains anaerobic work capacity at a power output continuous rowing never reaches.; Loads upper and lower body in the same interval, which running and cycling intervals do not.; Stays non-impact, so repeated hard efforts cost the joints far less than sprint running.
useCases: Interval blocks inside a rowing or hybrid conditioning program.; Machine-specific HIIT templates that need an on-screen movement reference.; Onboarding flows that teach stroke sequence before an app prescribes hard efforts.; Comparison content showing interval, steady state and sprint rowing side by side.
instructions: 1. Strap your feet in and set the damper to a moderate setting so the stroke stays quick rather than heavy. ; 2. Row easy for a few minutes, then settle at the catch with shins vertical, arms straight and shoulders ahead of the hips. ; 3. Start the work bout by driving the legs down hard while the arms stay straight until the legs are almost flat. ; 4. Swing the back open from the hips and pull the handle in to the bottom of the ribs to finish the stroke. ; 5. Send the hands away first, hinge the body forward, then let the knees bend and slide back to the catch. ; 6. Hold that sequence for the full work bout, then drop to light paddling for the recovery and repeat.
commonMistakes: Opening the back at the same time as the legs, which strains the lower back and leaks power out of the drive.; Rushing the recovery to match the drive, which shortens the next stroke and burns you out before the bout ends.; Chasing stroke rate instead of split, so the rate climbs while the pace on the monitor gets slower.; Sitting still through the rest, which slows waste clearance and leaves the legs heavy for the next effort.
shortDescription: Repeated hard efforts on the rowing machine separated by easy paddling, with stroke sequence held under fatigue.
longDescription:
Rowing intervals run the same four-phase stroke as continuous rowing at a pace you could not hold for a whole piece. Each drive starts with the legs, adds the back swing, then finishes with the arms, and the recovery reverses that order at half the speed. Rowing is a pushing sport far more than a pulling one, and intervals are where that breaks first, because tired rowers open the back and the legs together.

Interval work means short hard bouts with active recovery between them, and the erg suits that because pieces can be set by distance or by time.

In a product this clip fills the interval slot for rowing programs, pairs with steady state and sprint variants to complete an erg family, and gives interval templates a demonstration loop instead of a text label.

name: Steady-State Rowing Machine
tags: steady state rowing; rowing machine; erg; cardio; aerobic base; indoor rowing
benefits: Builds aerobic base below lactate threshold with no impact loading on the joints.; Recruits legs, trunk and upper body in one continuous pattern, unlike leg-only cardio machines.; Rewards a repeatable rhythm, which makes it easy to hold a target pace for long pieces.
useCases: Aerobic base blocks and long easy sessions in an endurance plan.; Stroke order tutorials taught before any interval prescription.; Warm up and cool down segments in erg based workout builders.; Default indoor rowing thumbnail for a cardio equipment browser.
instructions: 1. Strap your feet in so the strap crosses the ball of the foot, and set a moderate damper. ; 2. Come to the catch with shins vertical, arms straight, and the shoulders slightly ahead of the hips. ; 3. Push the legs down while the arms stay straight and the back holds its angle. ; 4. Once the legs are nearly flat, swing the back open and draw the handle to the bottom of the ribs. ; 5. Extend the arms away, hinge the torso forward, then bend the knees and slide back to the catch. ; 6. Repeat at a rate you can sustain, taking about twice as long on the recovery as on the drive.
commonMistakes: Pushing the legs and leaning back at once, which is inefficient and loads the lower back.; Recovering as fast as you drive, which cuts the next stroke short and raises the rate for no extra pace.; Pulling the handle high to the collarbone, which puts the finish above the strong line of the ribs.; Setting the damper at maximum, which turns a rhythmic aerobic piece into slow heavy pulling.
shortDescription: Continuous rowing at a steady sustainable pace, holding one rhythm and one stroke rate for the whole piece.
longDescription:
Steady-state rowing is the base version of the stroke: catch, drive, finish, recovery, repeated at a rate you can hold for the whole session. A workable starting rate is sixteen to twenty-two strokes per minute, with the recovery taking about twice as long as the drive. The legs push first, the back swings open, the arms finish, and the pattern reverses on the way back to the catch.

Steady-state work is continuous effort held below lactate threshold, and a sensible build runs from about ten minutes toward thirty, which makes the erg an easy entry point.

For a catalog this is the reference rowing clip. It anchors the erg family, works as the default library thumbnail for indoor rowing, and gives beginner programs a technique demo the interval and sprint variants build on.

name: Rowing Sprint
tags: rowing sprint; erg sprint; indoor rowing; power; anaerobic; cardio
benefits: Develops peak power output on a non-impact machine that measures every stroke.; Stresses the anaerobic system hard in efforts short enough to fit any session.; Reveals technique breakdown quickly, which makes it useful as a coaching diagnostic.
useCases: Maximal-effort segments in erg-based conditioning and testing protocols.; Power and sprint blocks inside a hybrid training app.; Intensity ladders that need visually distinct easy, moderate and all-out rowing clips.; Coaching content on why stroke rate and pace diverge at maximum effort.
instructions: 1. Strap in, set a moderate to firm damper, and row easy for several minutes before any hard effort. ; 2. Sit at the catch with shins vertical, arms straight and the torso hinged forward from the hips. ; 3. Drive the legs down as hard as you can while keeping the arms straight and the back angle fixed. ; 4. Snap the back open and pull the handle to the ribs, finishing the stroke with the legs already flat. ; 5. Push the hands away fast, rock the torso over, and let the knees rise into the next catch without collapsing. ; 6. Hold maximum effort for the planned distance or time, then paddle very light until breathing settles.
commonMistakes: Letting the recovery speed match the drive, which shortens the stroke and drops pace while the rate climbs.; Yanking with the arms before the legs finish, which cuts the strongest part of the drive out of the stroke.; Pushing the legs and opening the back at the same moment, which is inefficient and loads the lower back.; Judging the effort by stroke rate on the monitor rather than split, so the numbers rise but the pace slows.
shortDescription: An all-out short rowing effort where stroke rate and leg drive peak together and technique has to survive it.
longDescription:
A rowing sprint is the stroke at maximum power output. The leg drive is violent, the back swing sharp, the arms fast, but the sequence is unchanged: legs, back, arms in, then hands away, body over, knees bend. At sprint rates the recovery gets compressed first, and once it matches the drive the stroke shortens and pace falls even as the rate climbs.

The sequence has to be comfortable before it can be raced. Manufacturer guidance is to hold slower rating work until the fundamentals are solid, so a sprint belongs after the stroke is learned rather than during it.

As an asset it covers the top-end effort in an erg family, gives sprint conditioning content a believable maximal-effort loop, and lets a library show visible intensity differences between three rowing modes on one machine.

name: Running Cooldown
tags: running cooldown; easy run; active recovery; cardio; recovery; jogging
benefits: Speeds the clearance of lactate from the blood compared with stopping and standing still.; Provides a controlled transition out of hard work without adding meaningful training load.; Gives a low-effort segment that can be repeated daily without interfering with adaptation.
useCases: Closing segment of a guided run in a training app.; Recovery-day sessions that need an easy running clip rather than a hard one.; Session builders that require a distinct cool-down asset alongside warm-up and work blocks.; Educational content on what an active cool-down does and does not achieve.
instructions: 1. Finish the hard effort and keep moving instead of stopping, dropping straight into an easy jog. ; 2. Shorten your stride and let cadence settle to a rhythm you could hold in conversation. ; 3. Keep the torso tall and the shoulders loose, with the arms swinging low and relaxed. ; 4. Land under the hips with a quiet foot strike rather than reaching out in front. ; 5. Hold the easy pace for several minutes until breathing and heart rate come down. ; 6. Finish by walking for a minute or two before you stop moving entirely.
commonMistakes: Running the cool-down too fast, which keeps the session hard and defeats the purpose of the segment.; Stopping abruptly after a hard effort, which leaves you standing still with blood pooled in the legs.; Treating the cool-down as injury prevention, which the evidence does not support and can mask real issues.; Cutting it to under a minute, which is too short for heart rate and breathing to actually settle.
shortDescription: An easy jog after hard running, held at a conversational effort to bring heart rate and breathing back down.
longDescription:
A running cool-down is the same gait pattern at much lower intensity. Stride shortens and ground contact softens, but the working muscles are unchanged: the vastus group at the knee, the gluteal muscles and iliopsoas at the hip, and soleus and gastrocnemius at the ankle.

The evidence is narrower than the habit suggests. A narrative review found that active cool-downs speed the fall of blood lactate but not muscle lactate, do not reliably improve next-day performance, and do not prevent injuries, while also not blunting long-term adaptation. It is a sensible transition, not a recovery intervention.

In a product this clip closes a running block. It gives programs a low-intensity loop that visibly differs from tempo and interval running, and fills session-builder recovery slots.

name: Running Intervals
tags: running intervals; speed work; vo2max; cardio; hiit; running
benefits: Raises VO2max through repeated bouts near the velocity that elicits it.; Accumulates more time at high intensity than any continuous run of the same duration.; Gives a clear structure to progress, since work time, pace and repetitions can each be adjusted.
useCases: Work-bout asset in an interval running session builder.; Speed blocks inside a periodized endurance plan.; Comparison sets showing easy, tempo and interval running at a glance.; Coaching content explaining why interval pace differs from race pace.
instructions: 1. Warm up with easy running until breathing has lifted and the legs feel loose. ; 2. Set a target work duration and a matching recovery duration before you start the first bout. ; 3. Accelerate into the work bout and settle at a pace you can only hold for the planned interval. ; 4. Run tall with a quick cadence, driving the hips forward and swinging the arms straight back and forward. ; 5. Ease down into the recovery and keep jogging or walking rather than stopping in place. ; 6. Repeat the work and recovery pairs for the planned number of repetitions, then jog easy to finish.
commonMistakes: Starting the first repetition far too fast, which makes every later bout slower than the first.; Cutting the recovery short, which turns a set of quality intervals into one long moderate grind.; Running every session as intervals, which stalls progress because easy aerobic volume also has to be built.; Skipping the warm-up, which puts calves and hamstrings under near-maximal load from cold.
shortDescription: Repeated fast running bouts with recovery between them, run well above the pace you could hold continuously.
longDescription:
Running intervals alternate hard bouts with recovery so total time at high intensity exceeds anything a continuous run allows. Common formats run repetitions of two to five minutes near the velocity at VO2max, four by four minutes among them, and one such session per week is enough during base building.

The recovery is part of the prescription, not a pause in it. Beginner prescriptions use short work bouts with active recovery and keep effort inside an aerobic range at first, because the common failure is handing an untrained runner an elite interval structure.

As an asset this clip gives interval programming a visibly hard running loop that reads differently from tempo and easy variants, and it fills the work-bout slot in session builders that already have warm-up and cool-down assets.

name: Seal Row
tags: seal row; barbell row; chest supported row; back; lats; horizontal pull
benefits: Removes hip drive and lumbar load, so the back muscles do the work.; Enforces a repeatable range because the torso cannot shift between reps.; Trains mid-back thickness alongside the lats in one horizontal pull.
useCases: Back day blocks in a hypertrophy plan inside a training app.; A low-back-friendly row option in return-to-lifting programming.; Form explainer content where strict rowing technique is the point.; Pull-day library entries that need a chest supported row demo.
instructions: 1. Raise a flat bench on blocks or plates until a loaded bar clears the floor at arm's length. ; 2. Lie face down with your chest on the pad and your head past the end of the bench. ; 3. Take an overhand grip a little wider than your shoulders and hang the bar with straight arms. ; 4. Pull your shoulder blades together and drive your elbows up until the bar reaches the bench. ; 5. Hold the top for a beat without lifting your chest away from the pad. ; 6. commonMistakes: Peeling your chest off the pad to finish a rep, which puts back the momentum the bench position exists to remove.; Setting the bench too low, so the bar hits the floor and the bottom of every rep is cut short.; Leading with the hands instead of the elbows, which hands the work to the biceps and starves the mid-back.; Dropping the bar quickly on the way down, which loses tension in the lats over most of the range.
shortDescription: Strict barbell row performed face down on a raised bench so the hips and lower back stay out of the lift.
longDescription:
The seal row is a barbell row done face down on a bench raised high enough for the plates to clear the floor. With the chest pinned to the pad, the hips and lower back are taken out of the movement, so each rep is produced by shoulder extension and scapular retraction. That loads the lats together with the middle trapezius and rhomboids, while the biceps and rear deltoids assist. Free bent-over rowing carries the largest lumbar spine load of the common rowing variations, which is the reason chest supported versions exist.

In an asset library this is the strict rowing clip. The fixed torso and unbroken range read clearly at small player sizes, so it works in form guides, in hypertrophy back blocks, and as the row a program offers when the lower back is already loaded elsewhere in the week.

name: Seated Calf Raise
tags: seated calf raise; dumbbell; calves; soleus; plantar flexion; isolation
benefits: The bent knee shifts work onto the soleus, which straight-leg calf work under-trains.; One dumbbell per leg replaces a dedicated seated calf machine.; The seated position removes balance, so the ankle can move through full range.
useCases: Home-gym calf option for users with dumbbells and no calf machine.; Calf specialization block in lower body templates.; Content explaining bent knee against straight knee calf training.; Machine-free substitution for the seated calf raise station.
instructions: 1. Sit on a bench or box with your feet flat and your knees bent to about 90 degrees. ; 2. Rest a dumbbell vertically on each thigh, close to the knee. ; 3. Hold the dumbbells steady with your hands and sit tall. ; 4. Place the balls of your feet on a low block if you have one. ; 5. Let your heels drop until the calves are fully stretched. ; 6. Push through the balls of your feet, squeeze at the top and lower slowly.
commonMistakes: Cutting the bottom short, which skips the stretched range the calves respond to.; Bouncing each rep, which lets the tendon do the work instead of the muscle.; Resting the dumbbells on the knee joint, which is uncomfortable and shifts the load.; Rolling onto the toes at the top, which strains the forefoot without adding range.
shortDescription: A seated calf raise loaded with a dumbbell across the thighs, biasing the soleus with the knee bent.
longDescription:
The seated calf raise works plantar flexion with the knee bent to roughly a right angle. In this version the load is a dumbbell resting across the thigh just behind the knee, with the forefoot on the floor or a low block. Heels drop into a full stretch, then push up as high as the ankle allows. The bent knee shortens the gastrocnemius so the soleus takes the larger share; with the knee straight the gastrocnemius sits at long length and does more. Training data shows far greater gastrocnemius growth from knee-extended calf work, while soleus growth is similar either way.

For a catalog the seated variant is the partner to a standing calf raise, and dumbbell loading keeps it available to home users with no calf station. It fits dumbbell filters and calf specialization blocks.

name: Seated Dumbbell Curl
tags: seated dumbbell curl; biceps; dumbbell; curl; arms; isolation
benefits: The supported back makes cheating obvious, so the biceps take the load.; Each arm works independently, which exposes side-to-side differences.; Needs only a bench and a pair of dumbbells, so it fits minimal home setups.
useCases: Beginner arm day entry in a mobile training app.; Hypertrophy accessory slot in upper body templates.; Technique media contrasting strict curling with cheat reps.; Minimal kit option needing only a bench and two dumbbells.
instructions: 1. Set an adjustable bench upright and sit with your back flat against the pad. ; 2. Plant your feet on the floor about hip-width apart with your knees bent. ; 3. Hold a dumbbell in each hand with your arms hanging and palms facing forward. ; 4. Curl both dumbbells toward your shoulders, moving only at the elbows. ; 5. Squeeze the biceps at the top without letting your shoulders shrug. ; 6. Lower the dumbbells slowly to full extension and repeat.
commonMistakes: Peeling the back off the pad to start the rep, which reintroduces the swing the seat removes.; Letting the elbows drift back behind the torso, which shortens the range at the bottom.; Dropping the weights quickly, which throws away half of every rep.; Shrugging at the top, which passes work to the traps instead of the biceps.
shortDescription: A seated dumbbell curl with the back supported, removing the swing so the biceps work through a strict range.
longDescription:
The seated dumbbell curl is the strict version of the standard curl. Sitting with your back flat against a near-vertical bench pad removes the hip drive and torso lean that creep into standing curls, so the only thing that can move the weight is elbow flexion. Both dumbbells hang at your sides with the palms forward, and the upper arms stay pinned while the weights travel up. Letting the elbows drift forward at the top brings in the front of the shoulder, which is a variation rather than an error; the strict version keeps them fixed.

For a library this is a foundational biceps clip and the natural default in any arm section. It fits beginner arm days, dumbbell-only home programs, hypertrophy accessory slots, and technique content showing where cheating creeps into curls.

name: Seated Leg Curl
tags: seated leg curl; hamstrings; machine; knee flexion; legs; isolation
benefits: Isolates knee flexion so the hamstrings work without the quads or hips joining in.; The seated position holds the hamstrings at a longer working length.; Machine guidance makes it straightforward to load safely for newer lifters.
useCases: Leg day templates in a gym floor training app.; Machine-only circuits for commercial gym programs.; Knee-friendly accessory work where loaded hinges are unsuitable.; Leg curl station entry in a machine equipment filter.
instructions: 1. Set the seat and back pad so your knees line up with the machine's pivot. ; 2. Sit back with your thighs flat and the lap pad locked down over them. ; 3. Rest your lower legs on top of the roller, contact just above the ankles. ; 4. Grip the side handles and press your hips into the seat. ; 5. commonMistakes: Letting the hips lift off the seat, which turns the curl into a partial hip movement.; Locking the knees out on the return, which drops tension off the hamstrings.; Setting the roller on the calf instead of just above the ankle, which shortens the lever.; Snapping the weight back, which wastes the eccentric and rattles the stack.
shortDescription: A machine leg curl performed seated with the hips flexed, curling the ankles under the roller to load the hamstrings.
longDescription:
The seated leg curl is knee flexion against a machine. You sit with your thighs pinned under a lap pad, the roller resting just above your ankles and your knees lined up with the machine's pivot, then curl your heels down and back toward the seat. Sitting keeps the hips flexed, which holds the hamstrings at a longer working length than the lying version does. Sloppy technique on the lying version drags the lumbar extensors into the work; the seated setup, with the spine against a backrest, largely removes that risk.

In a catalog this is the standard machine hamstring entry. It fits leg day templates, machine-only circuits for gym floor apps, knee-friendly programming where a loaded hinge is not appropriate, and equipment filters where buyers expect a selectorized option.

name: Shadow Boxing
tags: shadow boxing; boxing; cardio; bodyweight; conditioning; combat
benefits: Trains a full-body kinetic chain in which the legs start the force and the arm finishes it.; Delivers cardiovascular work in timed rounds with no equipment and very little space.; Builds coordination and balance through combinations rather than single repeated actions.

All of the hinge is taken by one hamstring and glute, and the lateral hip and trunk work constantly to stop the pelvis rotating open. The sissy squat removes the hip hinge from a squat.
