benefits: Isolates the catch and pull so hand path and elbow position can be corrected without leg compensation.; Loads the main propulsive muscles of freestyle, which contribute the majority of forward force.; Builds upper-body endurance in a non-impact environment with no external load.
useCases: Drill modules in swim and triathlon technique programs.; Stroke libraries that split kick, pull and full stroke into separate assets.; Shoulder-health content explaining high elbow catch versus a dropped elbow.; Upper-body endurance blocks for athletes training around lower-body injury.
instructions: 1. Push off in a streamlined position with the legs quiet and the body long. ; 2. Enter one hand about shoulder-width apart, moving forward and slightly down, with the palm flat. ; 3. Set the catch by dropping the hand down and in while the elbow bends and points out to the side. ; 4. Press the hand and forearm straight backward as one surface, accelerating as the hand passes under you. ; 5. Finish the stroke just past the hip, thinking back and up rather than pulling straight through. ; 6. Recover the arm forward while the other side repeats the same sequence, keeping the legs still.
commonMistakes: Entering the hand too wide or too narrow, which compromises every phase that follows.; Rushing the catch and overpowering it, so the arm never gets oriented backward for the pull.; Sculling side to side instead of pressing straight back, which moves water sideways rather than behind you.; Dropping the elbow below the hand, a position linked to painful shoulders in competitive swimmers.
shortDescription: An arms-only freestyle drill that isolates the catch and pull so the underwater stroke can be rebuilt.
longDescription:
A pull drill removes the legs so the underwater arm stroke can be worked on its own. The hand enters about shoulder-width and slightly downward, then the catch drops the hand down and in while the elbow bends and points out to the side. From there the pull presses a large surface straight backward with increasing hand speed, and the hand exits just past the hip.

The muscles follow that sequence. Early pull-through is driven by pectoralis major, and late pull-through brings latissimus dorsi in to extend the shoulder. Pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi and teres major are the main force producers across this phase.

For a product this clip is the pull half of a swim technique set. It pairs with a kick drill and a full stroke asset, and gives shoulder content a reference for a high elbow catch.

name: Swim Sprint Intervals
tags: swim sprint intervals; freestyle sprint; swimming; anaerobic; cardio; intervals
benefits: Drives the anaerobic contribution that short freestyle events depend on.; Produces higher blood lactate than a continuous swim of comparable distance.; Trains speed and turnover under fatigue while remaining a non-impact activity.
useCases: Sprint sets inside a swim or triathlon interval builder.; Intensity ladders that need drill, steady and sprint swimming clips side by side.; Performance content on stroke rate and stroke length trade-offs.; Testing protocols that use short maximal repeats as a benchmark.
instructions: 1. Warm up with easy swimming and a few build efforts before the first sprint repeat. ; 2. Start each repeat from the wall and accelerate to full speed within the first few strokes. ; 3. Hold a high stroke rate while still pressing the hand and forearm straight backward on every stroke. ; 4. Keep the head steady and breathe as little as the distance allows without losing form. ; 5. Finish the repeat at full effort into the wall rather than easing off over the last meters. ; 6. Take the full prescribed rest, then repeat for the planned number of sprints.
commonMistakes: Letting stroke length collapse as rate climbs, which raises effort without raising speed.; Cutting the rest short, which turns a sprint set into a moderate threshold swim.; Breathing every stroke through a short sprint, which disrupts body position and slows the swim.; Sprinting before the shoulders are warm, which loads the pull muscles hard from cold.
shortDescription: Short maximal freestyle repeats with fixed rest, swum at a stroke rate no continuous swim can sustain.
longDescription:
Swim sprint intervals are full stroke freestyle at maximum effort over short repeats. A studied set of four by fifty meters with two minutes rest produced blood lactate around fourteen to fifteen millimoles per liter, well above the ten to twelve seen in a single hundred meter swim.

That is what makes the format hard to hold together. The propulsive muscles of the pull, latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major and triceps brachii, are the ones that fatigue first, and underwater EMG reviews find upper body fatigue during repeated hard efforts while leg activity stays comparatively stable.

As an asset this clip carries the high intensity end of a swimming set. It gives triathlon and masters programs a sprint reference distinct from drill clips, and gives interval builders a pool sprint loop.

name: Tate Press
tags: tate press; triceps; dumbbell; isolation; arms; accessory
benefits: Isolates the triceps at an elbow angle standard extensions do not cover.; Adds triceps volume without loading the shoulder joint overhead.; Light loads produce high tension, so it suits high-rep accessory work.
useCases: Triceps accessory slot in a hypertrophy program builder.; Bench press support work in a powerlifting app.; Arm day entry for libraries filtered to dumbbells only.; Technique content contrasting it with skull crushers and kickbacks.
instructions: 1. Sit on a flat bench with a dumbbell in each hand and lie back, keeping the weights close to your chest. ; 2. Press the dumbbells to lockout with a pronated grip and the inner ends touching. ; 3. Brace your abdominals and keep your ribcage down against the bench. ; 4. Bend the elbows and let them flare out to the sides, lowering the dumbbell ends toward your chest. ; 5. Stop when the dumbbells touch the chest, then extend the elbows to press back to lockout. ; 6. Squeeze the triceps at the top and repeat for your target reps.
commonMistakes: Letting the dumbbells separate, which removes the inward pressure the movement depends on.; Arching the lower back to help the press, which loads the spine and shortens the working range.; Going too heavy, which turns the flared elbow path into a shoulder-stressing partial press.; Dropping the weights fast, which skips the eccentric where most of the triceps tension sits.
shortDescription: Supine dumbbell press with the elbows flared out, lowering the dumbbell ends toward the chest.
longDescription:
The Tate press loads the triceps through elbow extension at an unusual angle. Lying on a flat bench with a pronated grip, you keep the dumbbells touching and lower their inner ends toward the chest by letting the elbows flare out to the sides, then press back to lockout. It is an isolation movement for the triceps, and keeping the ribcage down is what stops the lumbar spine overextending, with the front delts and chest offering secondary support.

As a catalog asset this is the kind of specific accessory that makes an exercise library feel complete rather than generic. Powerlifting and arm-specialization programs call for it by name, and the flared elbow path is easy to get wrong from a static image, so the animation carries real instructional weight.

name: Tempo Run
tags: tempo run; threshold run; lactate threshold; running; cardio; endurance
benefits: Improves the ability to clear lactate, which raises the pace that can be sustained.; Delivers a large aerobic stimulus without the recovery cost of maximal interval work.; Recruits faster motor units at a moderate metabolic intensity, avoiding excessive fatigue.
useCases: Threshold session assets in a running plan builder.; Middle-intensity slot in a library that also carries easy and interval running clips.; Coaching content on pacing and perceived effort at threshold.; Race-preparation blocks for half marathon and longer distances.
instructions: 1. Warm up with easy running for several minutes until breathing has lifted. ; 2. Lift the pace gradually into an effort you could hold for around twenty to thirty minutes. ; 3. Settle into a rhythm where speech is limited to short phrases rather than sentences. ; 4. Run tall with the hips forward and a relaxed upper body, keeping cadence even. ; 5. Hold that single effort for the full block instead of surging and backing off. ; 6. Ease down into an easy jog once the tempo block is finished.
commonMistakes: Running the tempo at interval pace, which turns a sustainable effort into a session you cannot finish.; Surging and easing repeatedly, which breaks the steady lactate balance that makes the session work.; Extending the block too quickly week to week, which outpaces the gradual progression the adaptation depends on.; Skipping the warm-up, so the first minutes are spent finding the pace rather than holding it.
shortDescription: A sustained run at threshold effort, fast enough to be uncomfortable but slow enough to hold for a while.
longDescription:
A tempo run sits at the pace where lactate production and clearance balance. The lactate threshold is the fastest steady state a runner can hold without fatiguing, and continuous threshold work is normally built from about ten minutes toward thirty. Reviews of distance running training put that zone at roughly two to four and a half millimoles per liter of blood lactate.

The mechanics are ordinary running held at an unusually disciplined effort. The vastus group, gluteal muscles and plantar flexors do the same work they do at every pace, and the adaptation targeted is improved lactate clearance rather than top-end speed.

In a catalog this clip is the middle rung of a running family, giving threshold sessions a distinct asset between easy and interval running.

name: Tibialis Raise
tags: tibialis raise; tibialis anterior; shins; dorsiflexion; bodyweight; lower leg
benefits: Strengthens dorsiflexion, which controls foot landing during walking and running.; Commonly used to reduce shin splint risk in runners.; Needs nothing but a wall, so it fits any home or travel program.
useCases: Lower-leg accessory block in a running or endurance app; Shin and knee prehab flow in a physio-adjacent program; Warm-up screen for ankle range of motion; Bodyweight exercise-library entry for home training content
instructions: 1. Stand with your back and heels flat against a wall. ; 2. Walk your feet a step forward so your body leans back slightly against the wall. ; 3. Brace lightly and keep your knees straight and your heels pinned to the floor. ; 4. Lift your toes and forefeet toward your shins as far as they will travel. ; 5. Pause at the top where the front of the shin is fully contracted. ; 6. Lower the toes back to the floor slowly under control and repeat.
commonMistakes: Letting the heels lift, which turns the movement into a rock rather than a dorsiflexion rep.; Bending the knees to gain range, which takes the work off the shin.; Dropping the toes fast, which skips the eccentric phase that gives the exercise its point.; Standing too close to the wall, which removes the lean and most of the resistance.
shortDescription: Wall-supported shin raise that lifts the toes toward the shin to load the tibialis anterior.
longDescription:
The tibialis raise trains dorsiflexion, the action that lifts the foot and controls it back to the ground on every step. Standing with your back and heels against a wall and your feet a step forward, you lift the toes and forefoot as high as they will go and lower them slowly. The wall-supported version is an effective builder for the muscle and responds to two to three sets of fifteen to twenty-five reps. It is beginner-level isolation work, and runners prone to shin splints are a group that commonly benefits from it.

For a catalog this is a small clip with outsized demand. Running apps, knee and shin rehab content and lower-leg accessory blocks all need it, and it is missing from most stock exercise libraries.

name: Toes-to-Bar
tags: toes to bar; core; abs; hanging; bodyweight; crossfit
benefits: Trains trunk flexion and midline control through a very long range.; Builds grip and forearm endurance as a by-product of the hang.; Develops scapular control and shoulder stability under load.
useCases: Advanced core entry in a CrossFit or calisthenics exercise library.; Top step in a hanging leg-raise progression ladder.; Skill-work block in a gymnastics-influenced program.; Technique content on strict versus kipping variations.
instructions: 1. Grip a pull-up bar slightly wider than shoulder width and hang with the arms straight. ; 2. Pull your shoulder blades down and back into an active hang and point your toes. ; 3. Push your palms into the bar so your head travels slightly behind your arms. ; 4. Brace hard and raise straight legs in front of you, keeping the ribs down. ; 5. Finish by driving the toes up to touch the bar between your hands. ; 6. Lower the legs under control to the hang without letting the body swing.
commonMistakes: Swinging into each rep, which replaces core work with momentum and destroys the hang position.; Failing to set the shoulder blades before lifting, which leaves the scapulae unsupported under load.; Bending the knees to reach the bar, which quietly turns the movement into a knee raise.; Attempting it before straight-leg hanging raises are solid, which is where lower back strain comes from.
shortDescription: Hanging from a bar, you raise straight legs overhead until the toes touch the bar, then lower them.
longDescription:
Toes-to-bar is the top of the hanging leg-raise progression. From an active hang you pull back slightly on the bar, flex everything and drive straight legs up until the toes touch, then lower under control. The rectus abdominis and hip flexors are the prime movers with the lats, forearms and scapular stabilizers supporting, which puts the movement in intermediate to advanced territory. It sits above the bent-knee and straight-leg hanging raises on the progression ladder.

In a product library this clip is what CrossFit and calisthenics apps come looking for, and it also anchors a progression ladder: pair it with hanging knee and leg raises so a program can route a user to the right step instead of prescribing a movement they cannot complete.

name: Towel Slide Leg Curl
tags: towel slide leg curl; hamstrings; slider; bodyweight; bridge; home workout
benefits: Loads the hamstrings eccentrically with nothing but a towel and a floor.; Holds the glutes in hip extension for the whole working set.; Self-limiting, so form breaks down before the load becomes risky.
useCases: Travel and hotel workout blocks in a mobile app.; Activation sequence run before lower body sessions.; Beginner posterior chain entry in a program builder.; Eccentric hamstring demo for catalogs with no machine assets.
instructions: 1. Lie on your back with a folded towel under each heel on a smooth floor. ; 2. Bend your knees slightly and rest your arms on the floor beside you. ; 3. Press through your heels and lift your hips until your body forms a line. ; 4. Slide both heels in toward your glutes while keeping the hips high. ; 5. Push the heels back out slowly until the legs are almost straight. ; 6. Hold the hips up throughout and repeat for the prescribed reps.
commonMistakes: Dropping the hips on the way out, which removes the hamstring load entirely.; Sliding out fast, which skips the eccentric that makes the exercise worth doing.; Trying it on carpet, where the towels grip and the slide stalls halfway.; Pushing through the toes, which lets the calves take over the slide.
shortDescription: A supine bridge with the heels on towels, sliding them toward the hips and back out under hamstring control.
longDescription:
The towel slide leg curl is the floor version of the ball curl. You lie on your back with a folded towel under each heel, bridge your hips up, then slide the heels toward your glutes and push them back out while the hips stay lifted. Any slick surface works, which is why the same movement shows up under slider, valslide and paper-plate names. The same pattern is usually taught with sliding discs, and it is self-limiting: the hips drop long before the hamstrings are dangerously overloaded.

For a library this is the zero-equipment hamstring clip. It fits travel and home program blocks, warm-up and activation sequences, beginner posterior chain templates, and content that needs to show eccentric hamstring work without a machine or a partner.

name: Trail Run
tags: trail run; off road running; hill running; running; cardio; endurance
benefits: Alternates concentric climbing work with eccentric braking, which flat running never does.; Loads ankle and hip stabilizers continuously because the terrain never repeats.; Raises cardiovascular cost on climbs while lowering oxygen demand on descents, varying the stimulus.
useCases: Trail and ultra running programs that need an off-road specific asset.; Content on eccentric strength and downhill running preparation.; Running libraries that distinguish surface and terrain, not just intensity.; Adventure and outdoor fitness apps building varied-terrain sessions.
instructions: 1. Scan the ground a few steps ahead rather than looking directly down at your feet. ; 2. Shorten your stride and lift cadence as the gradient steepens so each step stays controlled. ; 3. Lean forward from the ankles on the climbs and drive the hips through on each push-off. ; 4. Use the arms wider than usual for balance across roots, rocks and uneven footing. ; 5. On descents, keep the feet quick and light and let the knees absorb the landing under you. ; 6. Ease back onto an even rhythm whenever the terrain flattens out, then repeat as the trail changes.
commonMistakes: Overstriding on descents, which increases braking force and loads the knee extensors eccentrically.; Running downhill sections at race effort in training, which produces muscle damage that lasts for days.; Holding flat-ground stride length uphill, which raises effort without producing more forward speed.; Watching your feet instead of the trail ahead, which leaves no time to choose a line on uneven ground.
shortDescription: Running over uneven off-road terrain with constant gradient changes, alternating climbing and braking.
longDescription:
Trail running is defined by slope, not surface alone. Uphill sections raise activity in gastrocnemius, vastus lateralis, rectus femoris, gluteus maximus and the hamstrings, and runners raise cadence about four to five per cent while shortening stride. Downhill sections invert the demand: knee extensors work eccentrically to absorb energy and impact forces rise sharply, which is why descending carries most of the injury risk.

Posture shifts with the gradient too. Slope running studies record forward trunk lean and reduced erector spinae activity going up, and backward lean with increased lumbar lordosis coming down.

For a catalog this is the off-road running asset. It gives trail and ultra programming a clip that is visibly not treadmill running.

name: Trap Bar Deadlift
tags: trap bar deadlift; hex bar; deadlift; hip hinge; hamstrings; barbell
benefits: Produces greater peak force, velocity, and power than a straight bar at the same load.; Lowers the demand on the lumbar spine and hip compared with a conventional deadlift.; Teaches a hinge quickly because the neutral handles need less mobility.
useCases: Beginner strength tracks and first deadlift progressions in a training app.; Athletic power development blocks for team sport athletes.; Hinge pattern teaching content and form comparison articles.; Barbell collection pack merchandising alongside conventional deadlifts.
instructions: 1. Step inside the trap bar so the handles sit beside your hips, feet about hip width apart. ; 2. Send the hips backward and fold at the waist until the handles are within reach. ; 3. Take a neutral grip with your armpits directly over the handles and your shins near vertical. ; 4. Pull the slack out of the bar, brace your trunk, and squeeze your lats. ; 5. Drive through the whole foot and extend your knees and hips together until you stand tall. ; 6. Reverse the hinge and return the bar to the floor under control.
commonMistakes: Starting with the hips too low, which turns the lift into a squat and stalls it at the knees.; Letting the shoulders drift behind the handles, which drags the bar into the shins.; Rounding the upper back to reach the handles instead of hinging to them.; Yanking the bar off the floor before the slack is out, which spikes load on the lower back.
shortDescription: A loaded hip hinge pulled from inside a hexagonal bar, with neutral handles sitting level with the hips.
longDescription:
The trap bar deadlift lets you stand inside the bar and grip neutral handles at your sides, so the load sits closer to your center of mass than a straight bar allows. Biomechanical comparison of the two bars found the hexagonal version cut the peak resistance moments recorded at the lumbar spine, hip and ankle while raising the one at the knee, and it delivered more peak force, velocity and power across matched submaximal loads. In practice that makes it a hinge with more quadriceps involvement and less lower back demand, which is why it is so often the first deadlift taught.

For a library this clip is the accessible deadlift asset. It suits beginner strength tracks, athletic power testing content, and any program builder that needs a hinge option for people who are not ready to pull from a straight bar.

name: Trap Bar Shrug
tags: trap bar shrug; shrug; trapezius; traps; upper back; isolation
benefits: Loads the upper traps directly with the shortest possible movement.; Neutral grip keeps the load beside the body and off the thighs.; Simple to coach and easy to progress with small load jumps.
useCases: Trap and neck accessory blocks in strength app programming.; Equipment filtered library entries covering trap bar work.; Posture and upper back content for coaching platforms.; Pull-day finisher slots in program builder templates.
instructions: 1. Set the trap bar on rack safeties just below waist height and load it. ; 2. Step inside the frame and take the handles with a neutral grip. ; 3. Stand tall with a neutral spine and let the bar hang at arm's length. ; 4. Lift your shoulders straight up toward your ears with the elbows kept straight. ; 5. Hold the top for a beat and keep your head from pushing forward. ; 6. Lower the shoulders under control to a full hang and repeat.
commonMistakes: Bending the elbows to help the bar up, which turns the shrug into a partial row.; Rolling the shoulders around the top, which stresses the joint without adding trap work.; Jerking the load with the hips and neck, which risks the neck for no extra tension.; Stopping short of a full hang, which cuts out the range where the traps lengthen.
shortDescription: Neutral grip shrug with a trap bar, loading the upper trapezius through straight scapular elevation.
longDescription:
The trap bar shrug puts you inside the frame with a neutral grip, so the load hangs beside the body instead of in front of it and the shoulders can elevate without the bar dragging across the thighs. The single joint action is scapular elevation, driven by the upper trapezius with the deltoids holding the arms in place; surface EMG work on trapezius exercises found the shoulder shrug produced the highest upper trapezius activity. Because the range is short, the useful cues are a neutral neck, a controlled top hold and no ballistic jerking.

As an asset this clip covers a trap slot that plain barbell shrugs do not show well: the neutral grip and the frame around the lifter are visually distinct, which matters in an equipment filtered library and in pull-day or strongman flavoured program content.

name: Treadmill Run
tags: treadmill run; indoor running; cardio machine; running; cardio; gym
benefits: Sets pace and gradient exactly, which makes interval and tempo prescriptions repeatable.; Produces energy expenditure at the top of the range measured across ten indoor cardio machines.; Reproduces overground running mechanics closely enough for most training and coaching purposes.
useCases: Default indoor running asset in a machine collection or equipment filter.; Guided-run content where speed and incline are prescribed numerically.; Gym-based program blocks that cannot assume outdoor access.; Comparison content on treadmill versus overground running mechanics.
instructions: 1. Stand on the side rails, start the belt at a walking speed, and step on once it is moving steadily. ; 2. Build to your running speed in stages rather than jumping straight to the target pace. ; 3. Run in the middle of the belt with the torso tall and the gaze forward, not down at the console. ; 4. Let the arms swing freely instead of holding the rails, so the stride stays natural. ; 5. Land under the hips with a quick cadence rather than reaching for the front of the belt. ; 6. Slow the belt gradually at the end and walk for a minute before stepping off.
commonMistakes: Holding the handrails while running, which alters posture and unloads the stride.; Looking down at the belt, which rotates the body forward and weakens running posture.; Drifting to the back of the belt, which forces a rushed stride and risks stepping off the edge.; Stepping straight onto a fast-moving belt, which is where most treadmill falls happen.
shortDescription: Running on a motorized treadmill at a set speed and incline, with pace controlled by the machine.
longDescription:
Treadmill running reproduces overground gait closely. A meta-analysis of cross-over studies found spatiotemporal, kinematic, kinetic and muscle activity measures largely comparable between motorized treadmill and overground running, with small differences: foot-ground angle at footstrike about ten degrees lower and vertical displacement roughly one and a half centimeters less.

The working muscles are the same ones that carry any run: the vastus group at the knee, gluteal muscles at the hip, and soleus and gastrocnemius through push-off. What differs is control, since speed and gradient are set by the machine rather than by feel.

As an asset this clip is the indoor running default, belonging in machine collections and giving an indoor counterpart to the outdoor running clips in the same library.

name: Underhand Barbell Row
tags: underhand barbell row; reverse grip row; back; lats; barbell; horizontal pull
benefits: Underhand grip keeps the elbows in and biases the lats.; Trains a full hinged row pattern with heavy loadable equipment.; Builds the trunk and hip position control that free rowing demands.
useCases: Pull day barbell blocks in strength app programming.; Grip comparison content set against an overhand row clip.; Barbell only tracks for home gym users.; Lat biased row option in a back category browser.
instructions: 1. Load a barbell and stand with your feet about shoulder width behind it. ; 2. Push your hips back with soft knees and hinge until your torso is near 45 degrees. ; 3. Take an underhand grip slightly wider than your shoulders and set a flat back. ; 4. Pull the bar to your lower ribs with the elbows tracking close to your sides. ; 5. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top without standing up. ; 6. Lower the bar to straight arms under control and repeat.
commonMistakes: Rounding the lower back to reach the bar, which concentrates load on the lumbar spine.; Rising out of the hinge on each rep, which turns the row into a partial deadlift.; Curling the bar up with the arms, which leaves the lats and mid-back underloaded.; Jerking the weight with hip drive, which replaces back tension with momentum.
shortDescription: Bent-over barbell row taken with an underhand grip, which tucks the elbows and favors the lats.
longDescription:
The underhand barbell row is a hinged row with the palms turned up. The supinated grip keeps the elbows close to the ribs, so the shoulders extend rather than pulling out wide, and the lats take more of the load than they do in a flared overhand row. The middle and lower trapezius and rhomboids still work through scapular retraction, the biceps assist more than in a pronated row, and the trunk holds the hinge: free bent-over rowing was measured as the highest lumbar spine load of the common rowing variations.

For an asset library this is the grip variation clip. Paired with a pronated row it makes grip differences visible in explainer content, and it gives program builders a lat-biased barbell row for pull days without adding another piece of equipment.

name: V-Up
tags: v up; core; abs; bodyweight; obliques; home workout
benefits: Works the upper and lower abdominals in one coordinated rep.; Improves trunk control and balance without any equipment.; Scales easily by bending the knees or shortening the range.
useCases: Core finisher in a bodyweight or HIIT circuit; Rep-counted screen in an interval timer app; Ab-focused block in a home workout program; Bodyweight exercise-library entry for beginner-to-intermediate users
instructions: 1. Lie flat on your back with your arms extended overhead and your legs straight. ; 2. Point your toes, brace your abdominals and lift your feet a few inches off the floor. ; 3. Exhale and raise your torso and legs at the same time, keeping both straight. ; 4. Reach your hands toward your shins at the top so the body forms a V. ; 5. Inhale and lower your torso and legs together under control. ; 6. Stop with the feet just above the floor to keep tension, then start the next rep.
commonMistakes: Rounding the back and shoulders at the top, which loads the lumbar spine instead of the abdominals.; Swinging the arms to generate lift, which replaces core work with momentum.; Resting the feet on the floor between reps, which drops tension and makes each rep a fresh start.; Bending the knees to reach the top position, which shortens the lever and reduces the demand.
shortDescription: Supine core rep that lifts the torso and straight legs at once until the body folds into a V shape.
longDescription:
The V-up folds the body at the hips in one movement. From flat on your back with the arms overhead, you exhale and raise the torso and straight legs together so the hands meet the shins and the body forms a V, then lower without letting the feet touch down. The rectus abdominis and both sets of obliques are the working muscles, with the hip flexors, adductors and quadriceps assisting the leg lift. Rounding the back or swinging the arms shifts load off the abdominals and onto the lumbar spine.

As a catalog asset the V-up is high-volume inventory: bodyweight circuits, HIIT timers, ab-focused programs and home workout content all use it, and it needs no equipment in frame, so the clip drops into any visual context without looking out of place.

name: VersaClimber
tags: versaclimber; vertical climber; cardio machine; low impact; climbing; conditioning
benefits: Trains upper and lower body at once in a contralateral pattern, which few cardio machines do.; Delivers high intensity work with no landing impact through the joints.; Scales through stride length and resistance, so the same machine covers steady and interval work.
useCases: Machine-collection listings that want a vertical climbing option.; Low-impact high intensity blocks in a conditioning program.; Boutique studio content built around climbing machines.; Cross-training assets for programs that avoid running impact.
instructions: 1. Step onto the pedals and place one foot in each, keeping your body close to the column. ; 2. Take a handle in each hand at a comfortable height with a slight bend in the elbows. ; 3. Set a short stride length to start, so the pattern stays smooth before you lengthen it. ; 4. Drive the right foot down as the left hand pulls down, keeping the movement contralateral. ; 5. Reverse the pattern immediately so the left foot and right hand drive on the next stride. ; 6. Hold the rhythm for the planned duration, then shorten the stride and slow down before stepping off.
commonMistakes: Leaning away from the column, which pulls the body out of line and shortens the leg drive.; Starting with a long stride, which breaks rhythm before the pattern is learned.; Pulling only with the arms, which wastes the leg drive that makes vertical climbing efficient.; Setting resistance so high that the stride slows, which turns a cardio piece into slow grinding.
shortDescription: Vertical climbing on a fixed track, driving alternating arms and legs through a continuous upward stride.
longDescription:
The VersaClimber moves you through a vertical climbing pattern rather than a horizontal one. Feet sit in pedals and hands hold sliding grips, and the machine is driven by alternating limbs so one arm pulls down as the opposite leg pushes down. The demand is shared between the lower body and the upper body working together, with the core holding position between them.

Stride length and resistance set the intensity. Short fast strides push the session toward cardiovascular work, longer loaded strides toward muscular endurance, and both can be programmed as intervals or a longer continuous climb.

For a catalog the VersaClimber is a differentiator. Very few libraries carry vertical climbing at all, so this clip fills a genuine gap in machine collections and low-impact conditioning content.

name: Wall Ball
tags: wall ball; medicine ball; squat throw; power; conditioning; full body
benefits: Combines a full squat with an explosive overhead throw, training power through the whole chain.; Raises heart rate quickly, so it doubles as conditioning as well as strength work.; Improves coordination and throwing accuracy because every repetition has a target to hit.
useCases: Functional fitness and circuit content where wall balls are a standard station.; Power blocks in a strength program that need a full-body throw.; Conditioning finishers measured by repetitions in a fixed time.; Class builders that need one asset covering squat, press and cardio demand.
instructions: 1. Stand about two feet from the wall with your feet shoulder-width apart and toes slightly turned out. ; 2. Hold the ball at chest height with the elbows tucked under it and your chest tall. ; 3. Squat down until your thighs are at least parallel, keeping the heels flat and the torso upright. ; 4. Drive up hard through the legs and use that momentum to launch the ball at the wall target. ; 5. Extend the arms fully at the top of the throw so the release comes from the whole body. ; 6. Catch the ball on the rebound and absorb it by dropping straight into the next squat.
commonMistakes: Pressing the ball with the arms alone, which drops the target height and wastes the leg drive.; Cutting the squat short, which removes most of the power the movement is supposed to generate.; Catching the ball with straight arms, which sends the impact into the elbows and shoulders.; Starting with a heavy ball, which breaks the squat pattern before the throw is consistent.
shortDescription: A front squat into an explosive overhead throw against a wall target, caught on the rebound and repeated.
longDescription:
The wall ball links a squat to a throw. You hold a weighted ball at chest height about two feet from the wall, squat until the thighs are at least parallel, then drive up and release the ball toward a target roughly eight to twelve feet high. The catch loads the next repetition. Quadriceps and glutes generate the drive, shoulders and triceps finish the throw, and the trunk holds the torso upright.

Intent changes the prescription. Use a light ball for three to five repetitions for power, a heavier ball for six to eight for strength, and maximum repetitions in thirty seconds for conditioning.

For a library this clip earns its place as a hybrid asset, sitting in strength, power and conditioning collections at once and working as a full-body demo in circuit builders.

name: Wall Sit
tags: wall sit; quad exercise; isometric; bodyweight; home workout; leg day
benefits: Builds quad endurance and isometric strength with no equipment.; Reinforces a strong knee-over-ankle position under sustained load.; Trains mental grit and breath control under physical fatigue.
useCases: Leg-day finishers in bodyweight fitness apps; Home-and-travel workout programming with no equipment; Athletic-prep isometric blocks in performance tracks; Quad-endurance benchmark tests in coaching platforms
instructions: 1. Stand with your back flat against a smooth wall and your feet about two feet out from the wall. ; 2. Slide down the wall by bending the knees until your thighs are parallel to the floor. ; 3. Set your feet roughly shoulder-width apart with your knees stacked over your ankles. ; 4. Press your lower back firmly into the wall and rest your arms relaxed at your sides or out in front. ; 5. Hold the position with steady breathing as the quads burn, keeping the knees in line with the toes. ; 6. Stay in the hold for 30 to 60 seconds, then slowly slide back up the wall to stand.
commonMistakes: Setting the feet too close to the wall so the knees travel far past the toes, which overloads the joint.; Letting the lower back peel off the wall as fatigue sets in, which removes the quad isolation.; Letting the knees cave inward as the hold gets hard, which strains the joint.; Holding the breath to push through the burn, which spikes blood pressure unnecessarily.
shortDescription: An isometric squat hold against a wall that builds quad endurance and mental grit — the classic equipment-free leg burner.
longDescription:
The wall sit is a pure isometric hold that builds quad endurance with zero equipment. Standing with the back flat against a wall, the lifter slides down until the thighs are parallel to the floor, then holds the position for time. There's no movement, no equipment, no excuses — just the quads burning under sustained tension.

For app and content use, this clip is a staple finisher for leg-day workouts, an easy bodyweight inclusion for home-and-travel programming, and a strong piece for athletic-prep tracks where isometric strength matters. It also works as a benchmark test for quad endurance in coaching platforms.

name: Weighted Pull Ups
tags: weighted pull up; pull up; lats; back; vertical pull; dip belt
benefits: Extends vertical pull progression once bodyweight reps are no longer challenging.; Keeps the lats as prime mover while raising the absolute load.; Trains bracing under load because the extra weight punishes swinging.
useCases: Advanced tiers of a vertical pull progression in a training app.; Strength program templates that prescribe added load on pull-ups.; Calisthenics and hybrid content that shows loading options.; Bodyweight library entries needing a loaded progression clip.
instructions: 1. Load a dip belt with the prescribed weight and fasten it around your waist. ; 2. Take an overhand grip on the bar slightly wider than your shoulders and hang with straight arms. ; 3. Brace your abs and squeeze your glutes so the load stops swinging. ; 4. Depress your shoulder blades, then drive your elbows down until your chin clears the bar. ; 5. Pause at the top with the lats fully shortened and the neck neutral. ; 6. Lower under control to near full arm extension and repeat.
commonMistakes: Kipping the load up with the hips, which converts a strength rep into a swing.; Overextending the lower back to shorten the range, which loads the spine instead of the lats.; Adding weight before strict bodyweight reps are solid, which forces partial range reps.; Dropping into the bottom position, which puts the loaded stretch on the shoulders without control.
shortDescription: Pull-up loaded with extra weight on a dip belt, adding resistance once bodyweight reps are easy.
longDescription:
The weighted pull-up is the standard overhand pull-up with external load hung from a dip belt, so progression continues after bodyweight reps stop being hard. Mechanics do not change: you depress the shoulder blades, drive the elbows down and pull the chin past the bar. Surface EMG of pull-ups recorded the latissimus dorsi far above every other muscle measured, with the biceps brachii and infraspinatus next, then the lower trapezius, pectoralis major, erector spinae and external oblique, which is why the trunk has to stay braced rather than swinging.

For a library this clip is the loaded end of the vertical pull progression. It closes the gap between an assisted pull-up and a bar-only rep in a strength app, and it gives program builders a demo for prescribed added load in pull-day templates.

name: Wide-Grip Barbell Bench Press
tags: chest; barbell; bench press; wide grip; push; compound
benefits: Shortens the bar path, which some lifters use to keep pressing when a long range aggravates the shoulder.; Biases work toward the sternal chest rather than the triceps compared with a narrow grip.; Makes grip width a trainable variable, which is useful inside bench specialization blocks.
useCases: Chest specialization blocks in barbell strength programming.; Grip width comparison content for coaches and program builders.; Bench setup and scapular position technique libraries.; Barbell pressing entry in a browsable exercise catalog.
instructions: 1. Load a flat bench barbell and set the rack height so you can reach the bar with straight arms. ; 2. Lie back and take the bar well outside shoulder width, keeping it low in your palms. ; 3. Pinch your shoulder blades together and drive them into the bench, feet flat on the floor. ; 4. Unrack the bar with a spotter's help and let it settle over your chest. ; 5. Bring the bar down on a straight path toward the lower edge of your breastbone until it makes contact. ; 6. Press back up by driving your feet into the floor and extending your elbows, stopping short of lockout.
commonMistakes: Going wider than your shoulders tolerate raises collarbone and shoulder joint loading for very little extra chest work.; Losing shoulder blade retraction increases rotator cuff demand and shoulder instability during the press.; Bouncing the bar off the chest hides how much range you actually control and shocks the shoulder joint.; Letting the wrists roll back puts the bar behind the forearm and turns a chest exercise into a wrist problem.
shortDescription: Flat barbell bench press taken well outside shoulder width, shortening the range and loading the chest hard.
longDescription:
The wide-grip barbell bench press sets the hands well outside shoulder width, which shortens the bar path and increases the share of work done by shoulder adduction. Bench press EMG found that moving from wide to narrower grips increased triceps activity and decreased sternal pectoralis activity, so the wide grip favors the chest over the elbow extensors.

The trade-off is joint load. Musculoskeletal modeling shows wider grips raise acromioclavicular compression and glenohumeral reaction force, and that scapular retraction reduces rotator cuff demand.

As an asset this clip lets a catalog treat grip width as a real programming variable, supporting barbell filters, chest specialization blocks and technique content on bench setup.

name: Wide-Grip Barbell Curl
tags: wide grip barbell curl; biceps; barbell; curl; arms; isolation
benefits: Trains the inner part of the biceps that a shoulder-width grip works less.; Adds a low-cost variation to arm blocks that already use standard curls.; The fixed bar keeps both arms moving on exactly the same path.
useCases: Arm specialization blocks that rotate curl grip width.; Wide grip curl variation in a barbell filtered library.; Grip-width rotations across a training mesocycle.; Comparison content on narrow, standard and wide curls.
instructions: 1. Load a barbell and stand upright with your feet about hip-width apart. ; 2. Grip the bar palms up with your hands set wider than your shoulders. ; 3. Let the bar rest across your thighs with your elbows straight. ; 4. Pin your elbows to your sides and curl the bar toward your chest. ; 5. Squeeze the biceps at the top without letting your elbows travel forward. ; 6. Lower the bar under control to full extension and repeat.
commonMistakes: Arching the back to swing the bar up, which trades biceps work for lumbar strain.; Letting the elbows flare out with the wide grip, which drags the shoulders into the lift.; Keeping the same load as a shoulder-width curl, which breaks form at the wrists.; Stopping short at the bottom, which cuts out the stretched half of the range.
shortDescription: A standing barbell curl with the hands set wider than the shoulders, shifting emphasis toward the inner biceps.
longDescription:
The wide-grip barbell curl is a standard curl with the hands placed outside shoulder width. The wider grip rotates the shoulders slightly outward and biases the inner portion of the biceps. Everything else stays strict: feet planted, torso rigid, elbows against the ribs and movement only at the forearms. Because the bar sits wider than usual the wrists take an unfamiliar angle, so most lifters work lighter here than on a shoulder-width curl.

For a library this is a grip variation buyers filter for by name once they already own the standard curl. It fits arm specialization blocks, barbell equipment filters, hypertrophy templates that rotate grip width across a mesocycle, and comparison content on narrow, standard and wide curling.

name: Wide-Grip Lat Pulldown
tags: wide grip lat pulldown; lat pulldown; lats; back; cable machine; vertical pull
benefits: Loads a vertical pull in small steps for users without pull-up strength.; Keeps the lats as prime mover through a long overhead range.; Low skill and easy to coach, so it fits early program tiers.
useCases: Beginner back workouts in an app's machine based track.; Vertical pulling volume for users who cannot yet complete a bodyweight pull-up.; Physique focused blocks that chase lat width and pair pulldowns with rows.; Grip width explainer content built on sourced EMG findings.
instructions: 1. Attach a wide bar to the pulldown station and set the thigh pads snug. ; 2. Sit down and take an overhand grip clearly outside shoulder width. ; 3. Sit tall with braced abs and only a slight backward lean of the torso. ; 4. Depress your shoulder blades, then pull the bar toward your upper chest. ; 5. Stop when your elbows reach your torso and hold for a beat. ; 6. Let the bar rise under control to a full overhead stretch and repeat.
commonMistakes: Swinging the torso back to move the bar, which shifts the work off the lats.; Arching the lower back at the top, which trades range for spinal extension.; Starting the pull with the arms, which lets the biceps limit the set.; Pulling the bar behind the neck, which forces the shoulders into an exposed position.
shortDescription: Seated cable pulldown taken wider than shoulder width, pulling the bar to the chest with the lats.
longDescription:
The wide-grip lat pulldown is a seated vertical pull with the hands set outside shoulder width on a cable stack. You depress the shoulder blades first, then flex the elbows and extend the shoulders to bring the bar toward the upper chest. The lats are the prime mover in every studied version; the biceps, posterior deltoid and middle and lower trapezius assist, and the abs stop the torso arching back. EMG across seven pulldown variants found no significant difference in lat activation between wide and narrow grips, so grip width is a comfort choice rather than a different target.

As an asset this is the default machine back clip most libraries need. It anchors beginner pull-day templates, sits in cable equipment filters, and gives explainer content a clean reference for scapular depression.

name: Wide-Grip Pull-Up
tags: wide grip pull up; pull up; lats; back; bodyweight; vertical pull
benefits: Needs only a bar, so it fits home and outdoor program tracks.; Puts the lats in charge of a full overhead pulling range.; Scales in both directions with band assistance or added load.
useCases: Bodyweight and calisthenics tracks in a training app.; Middle rungs of a vertical pull progression ladder.; No-equipment program templates for home workout products.; Back category entries in an exercise library browser.
instructions: 1. Set an overhand grip on the bar noticeably wider than your shoulders. ; 2. Hang with straight arms so your arms and torso form a Y shape. ; 3. Brace your abs and squeeze your glutes to stop the legs swinging. ; 4. Depress your shoulder blades, then drive your elbows down toward the floor. ; 5. Pull until your chin clears the bar and the lats are fully shortened. ; 6. Lower under control to near full arm extension and repeat.
commonMistakes: Kipping with the hips to clear the bar, which removes the lats from the work.; Arching the lower back instead of pulling higher, which shortens the range.; Stopping halfway down each rep, which skips the stretched position where strength is built.; Adding reps with a partial range rather than regressing to band or machine assistance.
shortDescription: Bodyweight pull-up with the hands set well outside shoulder width, pulling the chin over the bar.
longDescription:
The wide-grip pull-up is an overhand hang with the hands set clearly outside the shoulders, arms and torso forming a Y at the bottom. You depress the shoulder blades, drive the elbows toward the floor and pull until the chin clears the bar. The lats are the prime mover, supported by the trapezius, rhomboids, infraspinatus and teres minor, with the biceps and trunk muscles assisting; EMG of pull-ups put the latissimus dorsi well above every other measured muscle. A closer grip recruits the biceps and chest more, which is why the wide version tends to allow fewer reps.

In a library this is the strict bodyweight back clip. It carries no equipment dependency beyond a bar, so it fits home and outdoor program tracks, calisthenics content, and any progression ladder that ends in a loaded pull-up.

name: Wide-Grip Seated Cable Row
tags: wide grip seated row; cable row; upper back; rhomboids; trapezius; horizontal pull
benefits: Biases the mid-back and rear shoulder more than a close grip row.; Supported seated position keeps the lower back out of the lift.; Constant cable tension across the whole pulling range.
useCases: Upper back blocks in app delivered pull sessions.; Posture focused program tracks for desk-bound users.; Grip comparison content set against a close grip row clip.; Horizontal pulling that offsets weekly pressing volume in upper and lower splits.
instructions: 1. Attach a wide bar to a seated row station and set the load. ; 2. Sit with your feet on the plate, knees slightly bent, and take an overhand grip outside shoulder width. ; 3. Sit tall, brace your abs and pull your shoulder blades down away from your ears. ; 4. Row the bar to your upper abdomen with the elbows traveling out and back. ; 5. Squeeze the shoulder blades together for a beat with the torso still. ; 6. Extend the arms slowly to a full stretch without rounding your back and repeat.
commonMistakes: Rocking the torso back and forth, which turns a back exercise into a hip movement.; Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears, which loads the upper traps instead of the mid-back.; Rounding the lower back on the return, which puts the lumbar spine under a stretched load.; Letting the weight stack pull the arms out fast, which loses tension at the end of the range.
shortDescription: Seated cable row taken on a wide bar, pulling to the upper abdomen with the elbows away from the ribs.
longDescription:
The wide-grip seated cable row is a horizontal pull from a low pulley with the hands set outside shoulder width. Because the elbows travel away from the ribs instead of tucking, the pull becomes transverse shoulder extension and the middle trapezius, rhomboids and rear deltoids take a larger share of the work than in a close neutral grip row, where the lats and rhomboids lead. The lats still contribute, the biceps assist, and the trunk stays upright with the shoulder blades depressed rather than shrugged toward the ears.

For a library this is the mid-back clip that pairs with a close-grip row. It gives program builders an upper back option on cable equipment, supports posture and pulling volume content, and shows a grip difference that is easy to see in a short loop.

name: Wrist Roller
tags: wrist roller; forearms; grip strength; isolation; accessory; wrist flexion
benefits: Trains wrist flexion and extension continuously through a full winding range.; Builds grip endurance that transfers to heavy pulling work.; One set loads both the flexor and extensor sides of the forearm.
useCases: Forearm and grip accessory block in a strength program builder; Finisher slot in an arm-specialization app; Exercise-library entry for armwrestling or climbing-adjacent content; Deadlift and pulling support work in a powerlifting program
instructions: 1. Load a plate on the roller rope and let the rope hang fully unwound. ; 2. Stand with your feet about shoulder width and grip the roller with your palms facing down. ; 3. Extend both arms straight out in front of you at about shoulder height. ; 4. Wind the rope up by rotating one wrist at a time, keeping the arms and body still. ; 5. Continue until the plate reaches the bar, then reverse the rotation. ; 6. Unwind the rope under control until the plate returns to the floor.
commonMistakes: Rocking the body or swinging the arms to help the wind, which takes the work off the wrists.; Letting the plate drop on the way down, which skips half the available work.; Dropping the arms toward the hips, which shortens the lever and makes the set easier than intended.; Loading heavy enough that the shoulders fail before the forearms do.
shortDescription: Hold a loaded roller at arms length and wind the rope up and down using only wrist rotation.
longDescription:
The wrist roller is a handle with a rope and a hanging plate. You hold it out in front of you at shoulder height with the arms extended, then wind the rope up one wrist at a time until the weight reaches the bar, and unwind it the same way. It is beginner-level isolation for the forearms and nothing should move but the wrists. The wrist flexors and brachioradialis are the prime movers with the extensors and pronators supporting, which is why one set covers both sides of the forearm.

As a licensed clip this fills a gap most libraries leave open. Grip and forearm accessory blocks, armwrestling content and deadlift support programs all want it, and the winding action cannot be communicated with a still image.

name: Yates Row
tags: yates row; underhand row; barbell row; back; lats; horizontal pull
benefits: Shorter range and upright torso allow heavier loading than a full bent-over row.; Underhand grip keeps the elbows in and biases the lats.; Less time spent at full hip flexion than a horizontal torso row.
useCases: Bodybuilding style back blocks in an app's program library.; Named variation entries that broaden catalog coverage.; Torso angle comparison content against a bent-over row clip.; Barbell-only pull-day templates for home gym products.
instructions: 1. Load a barbell and stand with feet about shoulder width behind it. ; 2. Take an underhand grip a little wider than your shoulders. ; 3. Push your hips back and hinge only until your torso passes 45 degrees. ; 4. Keep your chest up, a slight arch in the lower back, and the knees soft. ; 5. Pull the bar to your lower abdomen with the elbows tracking past your ribs. ; 6. Lower the bar to straight arms under control and repeat without standing up.
commonMistakes: Standing more upright each rep, which shrinks the range until the pull becomes a shrug.; Rounding the lower back to reach the bar, which loads the lumbar spine at its weakest position.; Curling the bar with the arms, which leaves the lats and mid-back underworked.; Loading for the shorter range and then jerking the bar with hip drive on every rep.
shortDescription: Underhand barbell row with the torso held just past 45 degrees, popularized by Dorian Yates.
longDescription:
The Yates row is a barbell row taken with an underhand grip and a more upright torso than a classic bent-over row, bent forward a little past 45 degrees with the chest up and a slight arch held in the lower back. The shallower angle shortens the range and lets you handle more load, while the supinated grip keeps the elbows close and drives shoulder extension, which is why lifters describe it as a lat focused row. The trapezius, rhomboids and biceps assist, and the hinge is still held by the trunk and hip extensors throughout the set.

As an asset this clip covers a named bodybuilding variation that programs and content still reference. It differentiates a catalog from generic row entries, works in pull-day templates, and pairs with a full bent-over row clip to show what the torso angle changes.

name: Z Press
tags: z press; shoulders; overhead press; seated; core; strongman
benefits: Trains overhead pressing with no leg drive or bench support available.; Forces the trunk and hips to hold a tall seated position under load.; Exposes limited overhead range that a standing press can hide with a lean.
useCases: Overhead press variant in a strongman or strength program builder.; Shoulder block for athletes who overuse leg drive on standing presses.; Exercise-library entry filtered by seated or core-intensive pressing.; Assessment clip for overhead range of motion in coaching content.
instructions: 1. Sit on the floor with your legs straight out in front and your torso upright. ; 2. Take the weight at shoulder height with an overhand grip and your elbows in front. ; 3. Brace your abdominals, squeeze the glutes and tuck the chin slightly. ; 4. Press overhead until the elbows lock and the ears line up with your biceps. ; 5. Pause at lockout with the trunk still vertical. ; 6. Lower back to shoulder height under control without letting the torso lean back.
commonMistakes: Leaning back to start the press, which turns it into an incline press and removes the core demand.; Letting the lower back round so the pelvis tips under, which blocks the overhead range.; Finishing with the weight in front of the head instead of over it, which loads the front of the shoulder.; Loading it like a standing press, which breaks the seated position immediately.
shortDescription: Overhead press performed seated on the floor with the legs straight, so the trunk gets no support.
longDescription:
The Z press removes every source of leg drive. You sit on the floor with the legs extended and the torso upright, then press overhead to full lockout and lower under control. Because there is no bench and no knee bend, the trunk and hips have to hold the position while the shoulders do the pressing, which makes it a shoulder lift with a large core demand. The shoulders are the target with the traps and triceps supporting, and the front deltoid is the prime mover.

For a catalog this is a differentiated overhead press asset: strongman and strength apps ask for it specifically, and the floor-seated position is instantly recognizable, so it reads as a distinct exercise rather than another shoulder press thumbnail.

name: Zercher Squat
tags: zercher squat; barbell; quadriceps; squat; front loaded; strongman
benefits: Removes direct axial spinal loading while still training a heavy squat pattern.; Forces an upright torso, which suits lifters who tend to pitch forward in a back squat.; Produces lower knee compressive force than an equivalent posterior loaded squat.
useCases: Advanced barbell and strongman tracks in a training app.; Squat option for lifters with shoulder or wrist restrictions.; Core under load and bracing technique content.; Barbell collection merchandising alongside front and back squats.
instructions: 1. Set the barbell in a rack at about waist height and step close to it. ; 2. Cradle the bar in the crooks of your elbows with your elbows around shoulder width. ; 3. Interlace your fingers with the knuckles facing up and stand tall with the bar close to your body. ; 4. Step back and take a stance slightly wider than your usual squat. ; 5. Break at the hips and descend with your chest up until your elbows reach the inside of your thighs. ; 6. Drive through the whole foot and stand back up, keeping the bar centered and tight to your torso.
commonMistakes: Setting the bar off center, which makes it slide sideways in the elbows under load.; Holding the bar away from the body, which loads the lower back instead of the legs.; Placing the elbows too narrow or too wide, which loses the shelf that holds the bar.; Training the lift while fatigued, since a failed rep with the bar in the elbows is hard to dump safely.
shortDescription: A squat with the barbell cradled in the crooks of the elbows, which forces an upright torso under load.
longDescription:
The Zercher squat carries the bar in the crease of the elbows in front of the body. That front loading forces the torso upright and lets the lifter reach a deep knee bend, so the quadriceps and glutes take the drive while the trunk, upper back, and biceps work continuously to keep the bar from sliding forward. Biomechanical comparison of anterior and posterior loaded squats found the front loaded version produced lower knee compressive force while recruiting the same musculature, and the Zercher position removes direct axial load from the spine.

For a catalog this clip covers the strongman end of a barbell library. It suits advanced barbell tracks, core-under-load content, and program builders that need a squat for lifters who cannot rack a bar on the back or shoulders.

name: Zottman Curl
tags: zottman curl; biceps; forearms; dumbbell; grip strength; arms
benefits: Trains the biceps and the forearm elbow flexors inside a single repetition.; The slow palms-down lowering builds grip and wrist strength.; Needs only a pair of dumbbells, so it fits home and travel setups.
useCases: Arm and grip blocks in a strength training app.; Dumbbell-only filter entry covering both elbow flexor groups.; Forearm development content for coaches and creators.; Time-efficient arm templates that pair biceps and forearm work.
instructions: 1. Stand upright with a dumbbell in each hand and your feet shoulder-width apart. ; 2. Let your arms hang at your sides with your palms facing forward. ; 3. Curl both dumbbells to your shoulders with your elbows pinned to your ribs. ; 4. Rotate your wrists at the top until your palms face the floor. ; 5. Lower the dumbbells slowly with the palms-down grip, taking three or four seconds. ; 6. Rotate back to palms up at the bottom and repeat.
commonMistakes: Rotating halfway down instead of at the top, which loads the wrist rather than the forearm.; Racing the descent, which skips the pronated eccentric that defines the exercise.; Letting the elbows slide behind the body on the way down, which shortens the range.; Using standard curl weights, which makes the palms-down lowering impossible to control.
shortDescription: A dumbbell curl that lifts with the palms up and lowers with the palms down, training biceps and forearms in one rep.
longDescription:
The Zottman curl fuses two curls into a single rep. You lift with a supinated grip so the biceps handle the way up, rotate the hands to palms down at the top, then lower slowly with the pronated grip, which puts the forearm elbow flexors in charge of the descent. It is an intermediate level curl with the forearms as the secondary target. The rotation has to happen deliberately at the top rather than partway down, or the wrist rather than the forearm takes the load.

For a catalog this clip earns its place because the rotation is the whole exercise and a still image cannot show it. It suits arm and grip blocks, dumbbell-only home programs, forearm development content, and any library that wants a single movement covering both elbow flexor groups.
